articles.summary: AI 投资热潮中存在两种截然不同的态度：唯我论者与愤世嫉俗者。即使你不相信 AI 真的“有效”，也依然可以认为它是一项好投资。文章探讨了这种将技术效用与投资回报脱钩的奇特市场心理。此外，作者还分享了关于恶意软件与被盗电脑、旧咖啡与熔化杯子制成的工业材料等杂闻。核心观点是，AI 领域的资本狂热并不完全依赖于技术的实际落地。
articles.summaryEn: There are two distinct attitudes in the AI investment boom: solipsists and cynics. You don't have to believe that AI actually "works" to consider it a good investment. The article explores this peculiar market psychology that decouples technological utility from investment returns. Additionally, the author shares miscellaneous news regarding malware versus stolen computers and industrial materials made from old coffee and melted cups. The core argument is that the capital frenzy in the AI sector does not entirely depend on the actual implementation of the technology.

AI solipsists and AI cynics (permalink)

As a technology, AI isn't exceptional. It's not exceptionally wicked. It's not exceptionally good. Take away the accompanying, galactic-scale stock-swindle, and we'd call AI's applications "plug-ins" and we'd use them and abuse them in the same way that we've used every other technology:
https://www.normaltech.ai/

As a destructive economic pathology, AI is extraordinary. AI boosters have spent a baffling and terrifying sum of money – over $1.4T, most of that in the past year – on the promise of making as many workers unemployed as possible, while lowering the wages of the meager survivors of this jobspocalypse. To make things worse, AI can't do the jobs it's replacing: AI is predicated on the premise that the monopolies, duopolies and cartels that control the global economy can deliberately worsen their products without suffering economic or regulatory consequences, because they're the only game in town.

In service to this bubble, AI companies have suborned regional governments into running roughshod over environmental and planning review in order to build endless acres of data centers, many of which will likely end up casualties of the imminent bubble-pop, never to be switched on or even completed. What an indignity to have your farm or house seized through eminent domain, only to see it razed and replaced by a weed-choked empty field, a lonely foundation slab, or an abandoned empty building that could only ever be repurposed for laser-tag or an ICE concentration-camp:
https://gizmodo.com/trump-on-data-centers-you-cant-fight-it-you-have-to-go-with-it-2000790014

This is just one of the many negative effects of AI that can be traced to the scale of the bubble. Were it not for the imperative to turn more than a trillion dollars of losses into a profit, we would not have the aggressive, site-destroying scraping epidemic. Nor would we see AI crammed into every part of every product and service we use. And of course, in the absence of the investment bubble, businesses wouldn't be firing productive workers and replacing them with defective chatbots.

The single most salient fact about AI is the investment bubble, not the technical characteristics of chatbots or recent advances in statistical inference. AI's investor story is an incoherent tangle of predictions about AI's future, ranging from the outlandish ("Once we spend enough money, AI will become God and solve all our problems, including our profitability crisis") to the dystopian ("The majority of jobs in the economy will be done by our chatbots, and the employers who previously employed those workers will split the wage savings with us").
None of these stories are plausible, which raises an urgent question: why have the world's wealthiest investors been so eager to hand over trillions to finance this bubble?

I have previously written about one reason that billionaires find the AI story so compelling: at root, many billionaires just don't believe most other people are actually, fully real. How could they? Achieving billionairehood requires that you inflict pain on vast numbers of people. If you truly believed that those people were as real as you are, you'd never be able to look yourself in the mirror. Whether it's Leona Helmsley's claim that "only the little people pay taxes," or Elon Musk's habit of calling people who disagree with him "NPCs," the whole ideological project of billionaireism is shot through with a kind of solipsism:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/05/fisher-price-steering-wheel/#billionaire-solipsism

This is true even in one-on-one encounters: for the Epstein Class, the children raped on his island weren't fully real – certainly not as real as their own children. It's even more true for the people that billionaires experience as statistical artifacts, such as Jeff Bezos's vast army of drivers and warehouse workers, with their sky-high on-the-job injury rates and the everyday indignity of their piss-bottles. It gets worse for social media bosses like Mark Zuckerberg, for whom AI's principal appeal is the prospect of ending socializing on social media, swapping your mulish friends for pliable chatbots who will organize their interactions with you to maximize your platform usage and thus the number of ads you see:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/19/billionaire-solipsism/#sirius-cybernetics

I think billionaire solipsism can account for much of the malinvestment in this obvious bubble, but I don't think it's the whole story. Rather, I think there's a whole cohort of investors who don't believe in AI, but believe that other people will believe in AI.

This is a well-established investment principle. As Keynes wrote, the point of investing isn't necessarily to pick the most beautiful contestant to win the beauty contest – it's to pick the contestant that the other judges will hand the crown to:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keynesian_beauty_contest

In other words, you don't get rich from stock speculation by identifying the businesses whose profitability will grow the most – you get rich by identifying the businesses that other investors will pile into, pushing the price up. All you need to do is sell your shares after the price spike, but before anyone else figures out that the business is a turkey. It's like that old joke: "I don't need to run faster than the bear (market), I just have to run faster than you."

From the perspective of a cynical AI investor, the question isn't, "Can AI do your job?" The question is, "Can an AI salesman convince your boss that an AI can do your job?" So long as enough bosses are convinced to fire workers and replace them with AI, AI valuation will continue to climb, and if they time the market right, they can get out before those valuations crash. This proposition gets even sweeter if the CEO of the AI company is in bed with financial regulators and stock exchanges, and can force your financial advisor to buy his worthless AI stock with "little people's" retirement savings:
https://fortune.com/2026/06/13/spacex-stock-index-funds-passive-investing-401k-nasdaq-100-russell/

A bet that bosses will fire workers and replace them with AI is a good wager. Bosses are absolute suckers for this scam. Bosses hate the fact that they can't translate their plans into action without first having a series of ego-shattering confrontations with workers who actually know how to do things, who insist that those plans are illegal, stupid, impossible or will kill people:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/12/normal-technology/#bubble-exceptionalism
For these bosses, AI is the chance to wire the toy steering wheel they play with all day directly into the corporate drive-train. With enough AI slaves, the boss can run the company all on their own:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/10/posthuman-as-in-no-humans/#hell-is-other-people

In other words, you don't need to be a solipsist to bet on AI. It is sufficient to believe that bosses are solipsists, who can be relied upon to empty the corporate coffers in exchange for worker-replacing magic beans.

This is true in many scam sectors. I'm sure that most of the people who finance the supplements that Andrew Tate and Joe Rogan hawk understand that they're just a way to give yourself very expensive piss. They don't have to believe supplements work to believe that there is an army of desperate and credulous young men who will give anything for the promise they dangle.

Likewise, you don't have to believe that Gwyneth Paltrow can help women "regulate their periods" and "correct their hormonal imbalances" by selling them rocks to stuff in their vaginas. You just have to believe that between patriarchy-induced body shame and patriarchy-driven medical neglect, there's an army of desperate women out there who will buy those rocks and risk their lives by sticking them inside their bodies:
https://web.archive.org/web/20181225035739/https://www.vogue.com/article/goop-jade-yoni-egg-lawsuit-gwyneth-paltrow-vaginal-pelvic-floor-health

AI is even worse than vagina-rocks, of course. When the bubble bursts, when the seven AI companies that make up 35% of the S&P 500 tank, when a third of the US stock market is vaporized overnight, our governments will reflexively turn to austerity, the go-to response to every financial crisis. Austerity is fascism's best recruiting tool:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/04/12/always-great/#our-nhs

When the AI bubble bursts, the defective chatbots that replaced skilled workers will disappear with it, leaving us scrambling to get that work done after the workers who understood it have retrained, retired, or exited the workforce. AI is the asbestos we're shoveling into the walls of our civilization and our descendants will be digging it out for generations:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/04/08/process-knowledge-vs-bosses/#wash-dishes-cut-wood

Long after the AI bubble bursts, we'll be dealing with its catastrophic carbon emissions. The Second Law of Thermodynamics isn't up for debate. Once we sink enough therms into the sea, we are losing the ice-caps.

AI is an ordinary technology, but the AI bubble is extraordinary: extraordinarily toxic and extraordinarily dangerous. The source of that danger is financiers, and they are motivated by a mix of solipsism and a belief in other people's solipsism. For them, the most exciting investment hypothesis is that "hell is other people":
https://locusmag.com/feature/commentary-cory-doctorow-hell-is-other-people/
(Image: Cryteria, CC BY 3.0, modified)

AI 唯我论者与 AI 犬儒主义者（永久链接）
作为一种技术，AI 并不例外。它不是特别邪恶，也不是特别好。撇开伴随其而来的银河系规模的股票骗局不谈，我们会把 AI 的应用称为“插件”，并像使用其他所有技术一样去使用它们、滥用它们：
https://www.normaltech.ai/
作为一种破坏性的经济病理现象，AI 是非同寻常的。AI 的支持者们花费了一笔令人困惑且恐惧的巨款——超过 1.4 万亿美元，其中大部分是在过去一年里——承诺让尽可能多的工人失业，同时降低这场就业末日中少数幸存者的工资。更糟糕的是，AI 根本无法胜任它正在取代的工作：AI 的前提是，控制全球经济的垄断企业、双头垄断和卡特尔可以故意恶化其产品，而不会遭受经济或监管上的后果，因为它们是镇上唯一的游戏。
为了服务于这个泡沫，AI 公司已经诱使地方政府无视环境和规划审查，以建造无边无际的数据中心，其中许多很可能会成为即将破裂的泡沫的牺牲品，永远不会被启用甚至完工。你的农场或房屋被通过土地征收权没收，结果却看到它被夷为平地，取而代之的是杂草丛生的空地、孤零零的地基板，或者一栋废弃的空楼，而这栋楼最终只能被改造成激光枪游戏场或 ICE（美国移民和海关执法局）集中营，这是何等的屈辱：
https://gizmodo.com/trump-on-data-centers-you-cant-fight-it-you-have-to-go-with-it-2000790014
这只是 AI 许多负面效应中的一个，这些效应都可以追溯到泡沫的规模。如果不是必须将超过万亿美元的亏损转化为利润，我们就不会面临这种具有侵略性、破坏网站的抓取狂潮。我们也不会看到 AI 被硬塞进我们使用的每一个产品和服务的每个部分。当然，如果没有投资泡沫，企业也不会解雇有生产力的工人，并用有缺陷的聊天机器人来取代他们。
关于 AI 最突出的一个事实是投资泡沫，而不是聊天机器人的技术特征或统计推断的最新进展。AI 的投资者故事是一团不连贯的、关于 AI 未来的预测乱麻，从荒诞不经的（“一旦我们花了足够的钱，AI 就会变成上帝并解决我们所有的问题，包括我们的盈利危机”）到反乌托邦的（“经济中的大部分工作将由我们的聊天机器人完成，以前雇佣这些工人的雇主将与我们平分节省下来的工资”）。
这些故事都不可信，这引出了一个紧迫的问题：为什么世界上最富有的投资者们如此急切地交出数万亿美元来为这个泡沫提供资金？

我之前写过亿万富翁觉得 AI 故事如此吸引人的一个原因：归根结底，许多亿万富翁根本不相信大多数其他人实际上是真实存在的。他们怎么能相信呢？成为亿万富翁需要你给大量的人带来痛苦。如果你真的相信那些人和你一样真实，你将永远无法面对镜子里的自己。无论是 Leona Helmsley 声称“只有小人物才交税”，还是 Elon Musk 习惯把不同意他的人称为“NPC”，亿万富翁主义的整个意识形态项目都充斥着一种唯我论：
https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/05/fisher-price-steering-wheel/#billionaire-solipsism

即使在一对一的接触中也是如此：对于 Epstein 阶层来说，在他岛上被强奸的儿童并不完全真实——当然不如他们自己的孩子真实。对于那些被亿万富翁视为统计数据的群体来说，情况更是如此，例如 Jeff Bezos 庞大的司机和仓库工人队伍，他们有着极高的工伤率，以及每天用尿瓶解决生理需求的屈辱。对于像 Mark Zuckerberg 这样的社交媒体老板来说，情况更糟，对他们而言，AI 的主要吸引力在于有望终结社交媒体上的社交，用顺从的聊天机器人取代你那些固执的朋友，这些机器人会安排与你的互动，以最大化你的平台使用时间，从而最大化你看到的广告数量：
https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/19/billionaire-solipsism/#sirius-cybernetics
我认为亿万富翁的唯我论可以解释这个明显泡沫中的许多错误投资，但我不认为这就是全部。相反，我认为有一大批投资者并不相信 AI，而是相信其他人会相信 AI。
这是一个公认的投资原则。正如凯恩斯所写，投资的重点不一定是选出选美比赛中最美的选手——而是选出其他评委将把皇冠交给的选手：
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keynesian_beauty_contest
换句话说，通过股票投机致富，并不是靠找出盈利增长最快的企业——而是靠找出其他投资者会蜂拥而入、推高价格的企业。你需要做的只是在价格飙升后、在其他人发现这家企业是个烂摊子之前卖出你的股票。这就像那个老笑话：“我不需要跑得比熊（市）快，我只需要跑得比你快。”

从一个愤世嫉俗的 AI 投资者的角度来看，问题不是“AI 能做你的工作吗？”问题是“AI 推销员能说服你的老板相信 AI 能做你的工作吗？”只要有足够多的老板被说服去解雇工人并用 AI 取而代之，AI 的估值就会继续攀升，如果他们踩准了市场时机，就可以在这些估值崩溃之前脱身。如果这家 AI 公司的 CEO 与金融监管机构和证券交易所同流合污，并且能迫使你的财务顾问用“小人物”的退休储蓄购买他一文不值的 AI 股票，这个提议就更诱人了：
https://fortune.com/2026/06/13/spacex-stock-index-funds-passive-investing-401k-nasdaq-100-russell/
押注老板们会解雇工人并用 AI 取代他们，这是一个稳赚不赔的赌注。老板们对这种骗局绝对没有抵抗力。老板们讨厌这样一个事实：如果不先与那些真正懂行的工人发生一系列伤自尊的冲突，他们就无法将计划付诸行动，而这些工人会坚持认为这些计划是非法的、愚蠢的、不可能实现的，或者是会出人命的：
https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/12/normal-technology/#bubble-exceptionalism
对于这些老板来说，AI 提供了一个机会，让他们可以把整天把玩的玩具方向盘直接接入公司的传动系统。有了足够多的 AI 奴隶，老板就可以完全靠自己来经营公司：
https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/10/posthuman-as-in-no-humans/#hell-is-other-people
换句话说，你不需要自己是个唯我论者才能押注 AI。只要相信老板们是唯我论者就够了，你可以指望他们为了换取能替代工人的“魔豆”而掏空公司的金库。
在许多骗局领域都是如此。我确信，大多数为 Andrew Tate 和 Joe Rogan 兜售的保健品提供资金的人明白，这些保健品只会让你拉出非常昂贵的尿。他们不需要相信保健品真的有效，只需要相信有一大群绝望且轻信的年轻人，会为了他们抛出的承诺而不惜一切代价。
同样，你也不必相信 Gwyneth Paltrow 能通过向女性售卖塞进阴道的石头来帮她们“调节经期”和“纠正荷尔蒙失衡”。你只需相信，在父权制引发的身体羞耻和父权制导致的医疗忽视之间，有一大群绝望的女性会购买这些石头，并冒着生命危险把它们塞进体内：
https://web.archive.org/web/20181225035739/https://www.vogue.com/article/goop-jade-yoni-egg-lawsuit-gwyneth-paltrow-vaginal-pelvic-floor-health
当然，AI 比阴道石头还要糟糕。当泡沫破裂，当占据标普500指数35%的七家 AI 公司股价暴跌，当三分之一的美国股市一夜之间蒸发时，我们的政府会条件反射般地转向紧缩政策，这是应对每次金融危机的惯用手段。紧缩政策是法西斯主义最好的招募工具：
https://pluralistic.net/2026/04/12/always-great/#our-nhs
当 AI 泡沫破裂时，那些取代了熟练工人的残次聊天机器人也会随之消失，而在那些了解这些工作的工人已经转行、退休或离开劳动力市场后，我们将不得不手忙脚乱地去完成这些工作。AI 就是我们铲进文明墙壁里的石棉，我们的子孙后代将花上几代人的时间来把它挖出来：
https://pluralistic.net/2026/04/08/process-knowledge-vs-bosses/#wash-dishes-cut-wood
在 AI 泡沫破裂很久之后，我们仍将应对其灾难性的碳排放。热力学第二定律是不容置疑的。一旦我们向海洋中排放了足够多的热量，我们将失去冰盖。
AI 是一项普通的技术，但 AI 泡沫却非同寻常：有着非同寻常的毒性和非同寻常的危险。这种危险的根源在于金融家，他们的动机是唯我论与对他人唯我论的信仰的混合体。对他们来说，最令人兴奋的投资假设就是“他人即地狱”：

blocks.text: 23rd July 2026 - Link Blog

The first known runaway AI agent - or a very bad marketing stunt? (via) Martin Alderson's commentary on the OpenAI accidental cyberattack against Hugging Face includes a couple of details I hadn't considered.
First, Hugging Face offers a truly rich target if you're trying to find potential vulnerabilities that require executing arbitrary code:

Hugging Face has an enormous attack surface. They have more interfaces than I can count which run untrusted models and code. While they definitely have invested in defences, by nature of their operating model they do have many more opportunities to be attacked than many other services. I certainly don't envy their cybersecurity teams.
Secondly, one of the things that has puzzled me is how OpenAI didn't notice that their sandbox had been so thoroughly breached by the agent. Surely they'd be monitoring network traffic closely?
Martin points out that:

It's also likely they were running a huge amount of benchmarks simultaneously with ~unlimited token budgets - you want as many samples as possible to figure out how good a model is at a certain benchmark. It may also be they are testing various different checkpoints of the model too, understanding how the model is improving as it goes through the various training stages.

The mistakes made by the OpenAI team running this benchmark are easier to imagine when you think about the scale at which benchmarks of this kind usually operate. For all we know they could have been subjecting a new model to dozens of benchmarks at the same time, in dozens of different environments.

blocks.text: written on July 24, 2026

Codeberg recently changed its
terms to
exclude projects that are largely written with generative AI.  Since I want
GitHub to face competition I have thoughts.

Codeberg is entirely within its rights to do this.  It is an association with
members and a democratic process, and that process produced a result.  But
democracy is a way of making a decision, not a guarantee that the decision is
inclusive, wise, or even good for the people already depending on it.  A
majority can still decide that certain projects and people no longer belong.

GitHub’s governance has never been democratic and there is plenty about the
platform that I dislike.  Yet democracy is not the main property I need from
infrastructure.  I need it to be predictable, dependable, and reasonably
neutral towards the legal Open Source software hosted on it.  A democratic
provider without a clear constitution can be worse at those things than a
corporation.

The actual wording makes this more difficult.  The terms prohibit
projects that
mostly consist of code written by generative AI tools.  In an actively developed
codebase, what does “mostly” mean, and who can still tell?  I could not reliably
assign authorship percentages to many of my own recent projects.  The line is
open to interpretation precisely where it needs to be enforceable.  In practice
the center will probably lose out, as it has a bias.

A harsher line would probably be preferable.  If Codeberg wants no LLM
involvement, it should say so.  If it wants to prevent autonomous repository
spam and abusive resource consumption, it should write rules for those instead.
The current middle ground delegates too much of the policy to moderators and
community norms.  I’m currently assuming the community around it draws a much
harsher social boundary, making projects and maintainers unwelcome even when
they technically comply.

It is a real shame that the Open Source and Free Software communities are
splitting this deeply over LLMs and agents.  There are serious questions about
copyright, labor, energy use, slop, and maintainers drowning in generated
contributions.  But these tools are also becoming part of how software is made.
The Open Source world needs to figure out how to engage with that future, not
just divide into camps.  More importantly, LLMs if done and used well, should be
welcome to all of us.  They could be used to reclaim control and power, away
from large corporations and institutions.

As I mentioned before, I want GitHub to face true competition in the Open Source
space.  I would particularly like some of it to come from associations rather
than another large corporation.  As a European project, Codeberg naturally
matters to me even more.  It can choose to be a smaller community with a
stronger political identity, but that is a different ambition from being a broad
and dependable European alternative to GitHub.

I wish Codeberg were more forward-looking here: willing to host the Open Source
software of tomorrow, not only software made in the ways its community approves
of today.  It has every right to make the choice it made, but I just do not think it
is a good one.

translations: 写于 2026 年 7 月 24 日
Codeberg 最近修改了其服务条款，将主要由生成式 AI 编写的项目排除在外。由于我希望 GitHub 能面临竞争，我对此有一些想法。
Codeberg 完全有权这样做。它是一个拥有成员和民主程序的协会，而该程序得出了这个结果。但民主只是一种决策方式，并不能保证决策本身是包容的、明智的，甚至不能保证对已经依赖它的人是有益的。多数派依然可以决定某些项目和某些人不再属于这里。
GitHub 的治理从来都不是民主的，而且该平台有很多我不喜欢的地方。然而，民主并不是我对基础设施的主要诉求。我需要的是它具备可预测性、可靠性，并对托管在其上的合法开源软件保持合理的中立。一个没有明确章程的民主化服务提供商，在这些方面可能表现得比一家商业公司更糟。
实际的措辞让事情变得更加棘手。条款禁止主要由生成式 AI 工具编写代码的项目。在一个活跃开发的代码库中，“主要”意味着什么，又有谁能分辨得清呢？对于我自己最近的许多项目，我都无法可靠地划分出代码的作者比例。这条界限恰恰在需要强制执行的地方变得模棱两可。在实践中，处于中间地带的项目很可能会吃亏，因为这种规定带有偏见。
划定一条更严格的界限可能反而更好。如果 Codeberg 不希望有任何 LLM 的参与，它就应该直说。如果它是想防止自动化的仓库垃圾信息和滥用资源消耗，那就应该针对这些行为制定规则。目前的折中方案将过多的政策制定权交给了版主和社区规范。我目前的猜测是，其周边社区划定了一条严苛得多的社会边界，使得某些项目和维护者即使在技术上符合规定，也会遭到排斥。

开源和自由软件社区因为 LLM 和 agents 而产生如此深刻的分裂，实在令人惋惜。关于版权、劳动力、能源消耗、低劣内容以及维护者被生成的代码贡献淹没等问题，确实存在严肃的争议。但这些工具也正在成为软件开发方式的一部分。开源世界需要想清楚如何应对这一未来趋势，而不是仅仅分裂成不同的阵营。更重要的是，如果 LLM 能够被妥善开发和使用，它们理应受到我们所有人的欢迎。它们甚至可以用来从大型企业和机构手中夺回控制权和力量。
正如我之前提到的，我希望 GitHub 在开源领域面临真正的竞争。我尤其希望其中一部分竞争能来自协会组织，而不是另一家大型企业。作为一个欧洲项目，Codeberg 对我来说自然更加重要。它可以选择成为一个具有更强政治认同感的小型社区，但这与成为 GitHub 的广泛且可靠的欧洲替代方案，是完全不同的目标。
我希望 Codeberg 在这一点上能更具前瞻性：愿意托管属于明天的开源软件，而不仅仅是其社区在今天所认可的方式下开发的软件。它完全有权做出这样的选择，但我只是觉得这并非明智之举。

articles.title: LLMs reward expertise
articles.summary: 大语言模型（LLM）让每个人都能成为通才，弥补了诸如编写 CSS 等技术短板，导致许多人认为使用 LLM 不需要任何技能。然而，要获得 LLM 能提供的顶级成果（如博士级别的数学能力），深厚的专业知识仍然不可或缺。文章指出，LLM 实际上是在奖励那些具备深厚专业知识的用户，因为他们能更好地引导模型并识别其输出中的错误。通才可以通过 LLM 完成基础工作，但专家才能利用 LLM 突破能力边界。结论是，LLM 并未消除对专业技能的需求，反而放大了专家的价值。
articles.summaryEn: Large Language Models (LLMs) make everyone a generalist by bridging technical gaps like writing CSS, leading many to believe that working with LLMs requires no skill. However, to achieve top-tier results that LLMs can deliver, such as PhD-level mathematics, deep expertise remains indispensable. The article points out that LLMs actually reward users with deep expertise, as they can better guide the model and identify errors in its output. Generalists can do basic work with LLMs, but experts can use them to push capability boundaries. The conclusion is that LLMs do not eliminate the need for expertise; instead, they amplify the value of experts.
articles.reason: 颠覆了“LLM 让编程门槛消失”的普遍认知，深刻揭示了专业知识在 AI 时代的真正价值。

blocks.text: In the 2010s, if you had technical gaps (say, you couldn’t write CSS), you had to either rely on a skilled colleague or just hope that the answer to your exact problem was out there on the internet. Today, everyone can write sort-of-okay CSS by delegating the task to an LLM. LLMs make everybody into a generalist.

Because of this, lots of people don’t think there’s any skill involved in working with LLMs. If you want the product that LLMs can deliver — PhD-level mathematics, pretty good but sometimes tasteless computer code, or awkward LinkedIn-style writing — you can simply ask for it. Since everyone is talking to the same models, “skilled prompters” are getting the same results as people touching LLMs for the first time.
This is wrong. The most important skill in prompting is expertise in the domain you’re prompting for.

A good illustration of this is Terence Tao’s conversation with ChatGPT about the recently-discovered counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture. This is not the same ChatGPT I talk to! I couldn’t get to where Tao gets, even with unlimited tokens to burn.
There’s a lot to learn about good prompting from Tao’s conversation. Here are a few observations:
Tao’s messages are very short and to-the-point. He doesn’t respond point-by-point to the model, just to the gist

The model outputs are much more concise than when I try and talk to GPT-5.6 Sol about mathematics. By signalling expertise, Tao shunts the model into “talking-to-mathematicians” mode, not “explaining-to-amateurs” mode
Tao pushes back when the model’s responses look wrong, but he doesn’t directly contradict; instead, he says things like “this looks more complex than I was hoping for”
Tao makes several leaps and suggestions himself. He almost never takes the model’s advice about where to go next

However, you can’t prompt like Tao on mathematical questions just by following these tips. The key to his technique is actually understanding the mathematics: pulling the relevant idea out of ChatGPT’s multi-paragraph response, suggesting alternate approaches or formulations, and identifying what “looks weird”.

Terence Tao is a better mathematician than I am a programmer. But the idea here — that domain knowledge makes you better at using LLMs — is something I’ve also experienced in my own work. If you have a good theory of your codebase, you can push the LLM much harder than if you have no familiarity. Because you have your own sense of what a good solution might look like, you can say “no, I think it could be simpler here”, or “but don’t we already do X?”, or “can we express this problem in these familiar terms?“.

This touches on an idea I’ve written about before: that system design problems are dominated by concrete specifics, not generic principles. Of course both are useful, but I’d rather have familiarity with the codebase than a deep general understanding of software systems. In his conversation, Terence Tao asks a lot of specific questions like “does X work here?”, or “given Y and Z, why A?“. I can’t ask those questions about the Jacobian Conjecture, but I can ask them about the systems I own at GitHub.

If you have no domain knowledge, you can cling onto the LLM to at least get something. That’s not bad! But if you have domain knowledge, you can wring far more value out of the same LLM by steering it hard in the direction you want. Most of us will have to do a mix of both these approaches, since we have domain knowledge in some areas but not others.

The usefulness of domain knowledge suggests that human expertise will continue to be useful even as models get stronger. For many tasks, the human is the bottleneck, not the model, because the difficult part is in communicating to the model exactly what kind of solution the human wants. The information is “in the model” already, but it takes a very smart human to pull it out.

translations: 在2010年代，如果你存在技术短板（比如不会写CSS），你要么得依赖有经验的同事，要么只能指望互联网上恰好有你那个具体问题的答案。如今，每个人都可以把任务交给LLM，从而写出还算过得去的CSS。LLM让每个人都成了通才。
正因为如此，很多人认为使用LLM不需要任何技能。如果你想要LLM产出的成果——比如博士级别的数学解答、质量不错但有时缺乏品味的计算机代码，或是生硬的领英风格文章——你只需直接提要求即可。既然大家都在和相同的模型对话，“提示词高手”得到的结果和初次接触LLM的人没什么两样。
这种看法是错的。编写提示词最重要的技能，是你所提问领域的专业知识。
陶哲轩与ChatGPT探讨近期发现的雅可比猜想反例，就是一个很好的例证。这和我平时对话的ChatGPT可不一样！即使我有无限的token可以挥霍，我也达不到陶哲轩的境界。
从陶哲轩的对话中，我们能学到很多关于如何编写优秀提示词的经验。以下是一些观察：
陶哲轩的提问非常简短且切中要害。他不会逐字逐句地回应模型，而是只针对核心要点进行回复。
模型的输出比我尝试与GPT-5.6 Sol探讨数学时要简洁得多。通过展现专业素养，陶哲轩将模型切换到了“与数学家对话”模式，而非“向业余者解释”模式。
当模型的回答看起来有误时，陶哲轩会提出质疑，但他不会直接反驳；相反，他会说类似“这看起来比我期望的要复杂”这样的话。
陶哲轩自己会做出一些思维跳跃和提议。他几乎从不采纳模型关于下一步该怎么走的建议。
然而，仅仅遵循这些技巧，你并不能在数学问题上像陶哲轩那样提问。他这套方法的关键在于真正理解数学：从ChatGPT多段落的回答中提炼出相关的思路，提出替代的方法或表述，并识别出哪些地方“看起来不对劲”。
陶哲轩作为数学家的造诣，远胜于我作为程序员的水平。但这里的核心理念——领域知识能让你更擅长使用LLM——我在自己的工作中也深有体会。如果你对代码库有很好的理论认知，你就能比毫无了解时更深入地挖掘LLM的潜力。因为你自己对优秀的解决方案长什么样有判断力，你可以说“不，我觉得这里可以更简单些”，或者“但我们不是已经实现X了吗？”，又或者“我们能不能用这些熟悉的术语来表述这个问题？”。
这呼应了我之前写过的一个观点：系统设计问题主要取决于具体的细节，而非通用原则。当然两者都有用，但我宁愿对代码库了如指掌，也不愿只对软件系统有泛泛的深刻理解。在对话中，陶哲轩问了很多具体的问题，比如“X在这里适用吗？”，或者“已知Y和Z，为什么是A？”。我没法针对雅可比猜想提出这些问题，但我能针对我在GitHub负责的系统提出这些问题。
如果你没有领域知识，你可以依赖LLM，至少能弄出点东西来。这也不错！但如果你具备领域知识，你就能通过强力引导LLM朝你想要的方向发展，从同一个LLM中榨取多得多的价值。我们大多数人必须将这两种方法结合起来，因为我们在某些领域具备领域知识，而在其他领域则没有。
领域知识的价值表明，即使模型变得更强大，人类的专业知识仍将继续发挥作用。对于许多任务来说，人类才是瓶颈所在，而非模型，因为难点在于如何向模型准确传达人类究竟想要什么样的解决方案。信息已经“存在于模型中”，但需要非常聪明的人类才能将其提取出来。

articles.title: Have you read it?
articles.summary: AI 生成的文章之所以糟糕，根本原因在于作者和读者都是在第一次阅读这些内容。当文章缺乏深刻见解时，读者提出的问题往往让作者不知所措，因为作者也是在和读者同一时间“发现”这些观点。文章指出，优秀的观点可以超越所谓的“LLM主义”，但 AI 生成的内容通常只是表面拼凑，缺乏真实的思考深度。作者因为忙碌而将写作外包给 AI，导致内容失去了与读者的真实连接。结论是，真正有价值的文章需要作者亲自参与思考与创作。
articles.summaryEn: The fundamental reason AI-written articles suck is that both the author and the reader are reading the content for the first time. When an article lacks deep insights, readers' questions often leave the author clueless, because the author is "discovering" these insights at the same time as the reader. The article notes that good takes can transcend so-called "LLMism," but AI-generated content is usually just superficial patchwork lacking real depth of thought. By outsourcing writing to AI due to being busy, the author loses the authentic connection with the reader. The conclusion is that truly valuable articles require the author's personal involvement in thinking and creation.
articles.reason: 一针见血地指出了 AI 生成文章缺乏灵魂的根源，提醒内容创作者不要盲目依赖 AI。

blocks.text: I think I finally figured it out. That is, the reason why AI written articles suck:
Both the author and I are reading the article for the first time.

When an article is insightful I don't even mind the emdashes or that the stark truth is not X, but Y. A good take can transcend even llmism. But then you have questions, and somehow the author doesn't even know what you are talking about, it's simply because they are discovering the insight at the same time you are.

They were busy, they didn't have time to write. As a consequence, they only dedicated enough time to skim the result before publishing. They don't know what's in it. You can't ask them what they were thinking when they came up with the insight because, well, they didn't think.
The great article sucks because there is nobody behind it.

blocks.text: Good morning premium subscribers! As ever, please ping me at ez@betteroffline.com if you have any questions.

Oracle has one of the strongest mythologies in the tech industry. Ask a regular person and they’ll tell you that it’s “incredibly profitable” and “growing fast,” that it’s “unstoppable,” and that Larry Ellison has the mandate of heaven with regard to the continual sales of software and hardware related to databases and AI.
And those people are completely and utterly wrong.

The original title of this article was “Is Oracle Dying?” because I assume, when I took a deeper look, that there’d be some sort of debate, some sort of bull case for a decades-old quasi-hyperscaler run by one of the more nakedly-evil CEOs in the history of tech. I assumed — incorrectly, I might add — that Oracle as a business was doing fine other than the ridiculous commitments it made to support the whims of Sam Altman and OpenAI via deals that I believed (and still believe) will kill Oracle.

Except it turns out that Oracle has already been on a death spiral for the best part of a decade (if not longer) and has only survived this long by screwing its customers, taking on masses of debt, and — most importantly — more than $85 billion in acquisitions over the last 23 years. Pretty much every major product line outside of databases is a hodge-podge of other people’s innovation stapled together with a legendary contempt for the customer. These acquisitions (and continual price increases) are the only thing keeping the reaper from Oracle’s door other than margin-destroying GPUs.
And that’s why Oracle’s revenue looks like this:

After April 2009’s $5.7 billion acquisition of Sun Microsystems, Oracle’s revenues barely kept pace with inflation until December 2021’s $28.3 billion acquisition of Cerner allowed it to create Oracle Health, adding about $6 billion in annual revenue that had 40% lower margins (about 21.7%) than Oracle’s other businesses, though Oracle immediately started closing offices and brutal layoffs to try and bring them up.
And as I mentioned above, Oracle’s other plan was to sink a little over $99 billion in capital expenditures since the middle of calendar year 2020 into AI GPUs.
Anyway, let’s see what that’s done to margins-OH MY GOD!

Oracle is a decades-long mission to keep reapplying lipstick to a pig. Billions of dollars of acquisitions have, for the most part, only succeeded in keeping the company’s revenue growth from going negative, and as noted by forensic accountant Howard M. Schilit, this is one of the most well-documented cases of accounting shenanigans being used to cover up that a business is in decline.

Today’s newsletter is a sequel to the Hater’s Guide To Oracle, where I told the sordid tale of how Larry Ellison grew a massive, lucrative business out of a database business that one reporter once told me was a “law firm with a database company attached,” an Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) product that competes with SAP to create the most-annoying way to run a large company, and a business built around licensing Java that exists mostly to email people and say “you need to pay us for Java or we’ll sue you.”

Then, as I’ve mentioned, there’s Oracle’s cloud infrastructure business, a decade-old also-ran that was meant to compete with Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services, but only managed to catch up following the advent of AI GPUs and a movement where all it took to party was buying billions of GPUs and saying “gosh darn, we love AI.”

I originally started drafting this as a much tamer piece where I’d ask whether Oracle was dying, but as my editor and I started digging into the research, it became obvious that not only is Oracle dying, it’s been dying for years, kept alive through decades of acquisitions and a desperate and dangerous commitment to generative AI.
And AI, I believe, will be what eventually kills Oracle dead.

In the past, all Oracle had to do to survive was buy somebody else’s company and replace its flagging revenues with theirs, turning the screws on their customers and laying off as many people as necessary to balance the books. While chaotic and decaying, Oracle’s empire has kept above water by never overextending itself, always keeping a positive free cashflow, and generally avoiding buying into industry hype cycles outside of whatever SaaS vehicle might potentially plug the gap in its earnings.

Yet with AI, Oracle broke its long-standing trend of letting someone else figure out the innovation, choosing instead to build its own cloud infrastructure, spending more in capex in its last fiscal year ($55.6 billion) than it did in the previous nine years combined ($50.4 billion), tripling its debt from $56.91 billion in FY2017 to $167.4 billion in FY2026, a year that ended with its free cashflow sitting at negative $23.69 billion.
For comparison, Oracle has had positive free cashflow every single year since 2001, including the Great Financial Crisis and COVID.

Oracle has doomed itself with its commitment to the AI bubble. It has committed to building 7.1GW of data center capacity for one company — OpenAI — as part of a $300 billion, five-year-long contract that requires it to build an impossible amount of capacity in an impossible period of time for a client that could never afford the $70 billion or more in annual costs to make any of it worth it.
Today I am going to talk trash on what I consider to be one of the single-worst companies in the tech industry that’s survived only through financial engineering and never, ever overextending itself.

With revenue plateauing and customers in revolt, Oracle’s future already looked murky, but with the power of AI — and $95 billion in FY2027 capex — it’s becoming increasingly clear that this may be Larry Ellison’s last dance with Silicon Valley.
This is the Hater’s Guide To Oracle Part 2, or AIpoaclypse Now.

Oracle 在科技界拥有最强大的神话之一。随便问个普通人，他们都会告诉你它“利润惊人”、“增长迅速”、“势不可挡”，并且 Larry Ellison 在持续销售与数据库和 AI 相关的软硬件方面仿佛拥有天命所归的特权。
而这些人完全、彻底地错了。

这篇文章的原定标题是“Oracle 正在走向死亡吗？”，因为我以为，当我深入观察时，对于这家由科技史上最赤裸裸邪恶的 CEO 之一运营的、拥有数十年历史的准超大规模云服务商，会有某种争论，某种看涨的理由。我曾假设——顺便说一句，这个假设是错误的——Oracle 作为一家企业，除了它为了满足 Sam Altman 和 OpenAI 的心血来潮而做出的那些荒谬承诺（通过一些我认为、并且依然认为会搞垮 Oracle 的交易）之外，其业务状况其实还不错。

但事实证明，Oracle 在过去近十年（甚至更久）里一直处于死亡螺旋之中，它之所以能存活这么久，完全是靠压榨客户、背负巨额债务，以及——最重要的是——在过去 23 年里进行了超过 850 亿美元的收购。除了数据库之外，几乎每一条主要产品线都是把别人的创新拼凑在一起的大杂烩，并伴随着对客户传奇般的蔑视。除了那些摧毁利润率的 GPU 之外，正是这些收购（以及不断的提价）才让死神没有敲响 Oracle 的大门。
这就是为什么 Oracle 的营收看起来是这样的：

在 2009 年 4 月以 57 亿美元收购 Sun Microsystems 之后，Oracle 的营收勉强跟上通货膨胀的步伐，直到 2021 年 12 月以 283 亿美元收购 Cerner，使其得以创建 Oracle Health，增加了约 60 亿美元的年收入，但其利润率（约 21.7%）比 Oracle 的其他业务低了 40%，尽管 Oracle 立即开始关闭办事处并进行残酷的裁员，试图提高这些业务的利润率。
正如我上面提到的，Oracle 的另一个计划是，自 2020 年年中以来，将略高于 990 亿美元的资本支出投入到 AI GPU 中。
无论如何，让我们看看这对利润率造成了什么影响——我的天哪！
Oracle 是一项长达数十年的任务，旨在不断给猪涂口红（指粉饰太平）。数十亿美元的收购在很大程度上只是成功地让公司的营收增长没有变成负数，而且正如法务会计师 Howard M. Schilit 所指出的，这是利用财务造假来掩盖业务衰退的最有据可查的案例之一。

今天的通讯是《Hater’s Guide To Oracle》的续篇，在那篇文章中，我讲述了 Larry Ellison 如何从一项数据库业务中发展出庞大且有利可图的企业的肮脏故事——一位记者曾告诉我，这是一家“附带数据库公司的律师事务所”；一款与 SAP 竞争、旨在创造运营大公司最烦人方式的企业资源计划（ERP）产品；以及一项围绕 Java 授权建立的业务，其存在的主要目的就是给人们发电子邮件说“你需要为 Java 付钱给我们，否则我们就起诉你”。
然后，正如我所提到的，还有 Oracle 的云基础设施业务，这是一个有着十年历史的落败者，原本打算与 Microsoft Azure 和 Amazon Web Services 竞争，但直到 AI GPU 的出现以及一场只需购买数十亿个 GPU 并高呼“天哪，我们热爱 AI”就能加入的狂欢之后，它才勉强赶上步伐。
我最初起草这篇文章时，语气要温和得多，只是想探讨 Oracle 是否正在走向衰亡。但随着我和编辑开始深入研究，显而易见的是，Oracle 不仅正在衰亡，而且已经衰亡多年，只是靠着数十年的收购以及对生成式 AI 孤注一掷且危险的投入才勉强维持生命。
而我相信，AI 最终将彻底终结 Oracle。
过去，Oracle 为了生存只需收购别人的公司，用他们的收入来填补自己衰退的营收，向客户极限施压，并尽可能多地裁员以实现收支平衡。尽管内部混乱且不断衰退，Oracle 帝国之所以能维持下去，是因为它从不盲目扩张，始终保持正的自由现金流，并且通常避免卷入行业的炒作周期，除非某种 SaaS 载体有可能填补其盈利缺口。
然而在 AI 领域，Oracle 打破了长期以来让别人去搞创新的传统，转而选择建设自己的云基础设施。在上一财年，其资本支出（556 亿美元）超过了前九年的总和（504 亿美元），债务也从 2017 财年的 569.1 亿美元飙升至 2026 财年的 1674 亿美元，翻了三倍，而该财年结束时，其自由现金流为负 236.9 亿美元。
作为对比，自 2001 年以来，Oracle 每年的自由现金流均为正，包括在次贷危机和新冠疫情期间。
Oracle 对 AI 泡沫的押注注定了它的毁灭。它承诺为一家公司——OpenAI——建设 7.1GW 的数据中心容量，作为一份价值 3000 亿美元、为期五年的合同的一部分。该合同要求它在不可能的时间内建设不可能的容量，而其客户永远无法承担每年 700 亿美元甚至更多的成本来让这一切物有所值。
今天我要来吐槽这家我认为是科技界最烂的公司之一，它仅仅依靠财务工程苟活，而且从不盲目扩张。
随着营收停滞和客户反抗，Oracle 的未来本已显得黯淡，但在 AI 的力量——以及 2027 财年 950 亿美元的资本支出——的加持下，越来越明显的是，这可能是 Larry Ellison 与硅谷的最后一舞。
这是《Oracle 黑粉指南》第二部分，或者叫《现代 AI 启示录》。

articles.title: Adding a backup Internet WAN on my OPNsense Router
articles.titleZh: 在我的 OPNsense 路由器上添加备用互联网 WAN
articles.summary: 由于 Spectrum 商业宽带连续两周出现故障，作者决定为 OPNsense 路由器配置备用互联网连接。方案使用了借来的便携式 5G 网关作为备用网络选项，以确保在主网络中断时保持在线。文章详细记录了在 OPNsense 中配置多 WAN 故障转移的具体步骤和测试过程。这种配置有效解决了单一宽带服务商带来的网络稳定性问题。结论是，利用 5G 网关作为备用 WAN 是提升家庭或小型办公网络可靠性的实用且低成本的方案。
articles.summaryEn: After Spectrum Business cable internet went down two weeks in a row, the author decided to configure a backup internet connection for the OPNsense router. The solution uses a borrowed portable 5G gateway as a backup network option to ensure online availability during primary network outages. The article details the specific steps and testing process for configuring multi-WAN failover in OPNsense. This setup effectively solves the network stability issues caused by relying on a single broadband provider. The conclusion is that using a 5G gateway as a backup WAN is a practical and cost-effective solution for improving the reliability of home or small office networks.
articles.reason: 提供了使用 OPNsense 配置 5G 备用 WAN 的实战教程，对追求网络高可用性的技术爱好者极具参考价值。

blocks.text: AKA "Spectrum has gone down two weeks in a row and I'm sick of it".

I've been borrowing a portable 5G gateway from my Dad for a few weeks, for testing... and two weeks in a row, I've used it as a backup Internet option, since my Spectrum Business cable Internet has gone down.

And yes, I'd get AT&T Fiber if I had the option, sadly they don't yet provide service at my studio. So I'm stuck with only one high speed wired provider. I may add on my own 5G backup Internet connection in the future, but we're getting off track.

The first outage, I unplugged my Cable modem from my ETH1 port, and plugged in the 5G gateway. I then rebooted the router, and also my main Mac (it's DHCP and DNS caching seems very aggressive, at least for Safari's networking stack).

That works, but it's quite inconvenient, because I had to keep checking on Spectrum's Internet status, then when it was finally back up, I had to walk back and re-plug my cable modem into my router, and reboot everything again.
Wouldn't it be easier if I could just... do it in software?
OPNsense and dual WAN
My plan was to plug the 5G gateway into 'ETH2' (the third Ethernet port on my OPNsense box; ETH0 went to my LAN, ETH1 was for the Cable modem, and ETH2 and ETH3 are available—all are 2.5 Gbps ports).
'ETH2' was device 'igc2', so I logged into OPNsense, and under Interfaces > Assignments, I assigned new interface 'igc2' named 'WAN2'.
Then I clicked on WAN2 in the sidebar, and changed the following settings:
Enable (checked)
IPv4 Configuration Type: DHCP
Click 'Save', then 'Apply Changes' (at the top), then go to System > Gateways > Configuration, and make sure your new WAN2 gateway has appeared there.
(Since I don't want automatic failover, I won't set up any specific rules / monitors here, but you can figure that out on your own if you want that.)
Go to Firewall > NAT > Outbound and make sure you have 'Automatic outbound NAT' set up. If it is not set up, you may need to add a rule for the WAN2 interface.
Failover
To actually failover to WAN2:
Visit System > Gateways > Configuration
Edit WAN2_DHCP, and set the Priority to "1" (and make sure it is not 'Disabled')
Edit WAN_DHCP, and set the Priority to "2"
Click 'Apply' and wait a few seconds
I usually use curl icanhazip.com or visit fast.com to determine which connection my computer's actually using at any given moment.
To switch back, set WAN2_DHCP to "2" (or more), and WAN_DHCP to "1" (making sure it is not 'Disabled'), and click 'Apply' again.

translations: 也就是“Spectrum 连续两周宕机，我真是受够了”。
几周来我一直在借用我爸的便携式 5G 网关进行测试……结果连续两周，因为我的 Spectrum Business 有线宽带断网，我都把它当作备用网络来用了。
没错，如果有的选，我肯定会装 AT&T 光纤，可惜他们还没在我的工作室提供服务。所以我只能被这一家高速有线网络提供商绑死。以后我可能会自己加一条 5G 备用网络，不过这扯远了。
第一次断网时，我把 Cable 调制解调器从 ETH1 端口拔下来，插上了 5G 网关。然后我重启了路由器，还有我的主力 Mac（它的 DHCP 和 DNS 缓存机制非常激进，至少对 Safari 的网络栈来说是这样）。
这样确实能用，但非常不方便，因为我得不断去查 Spectrum 的网络状态，等它终于恢复后，我还得走回去把 Cable 调制解调器重新插到路由器上，然后再把所有设备重启一遍。
如果我能直接……用软件搞定，是不是会轻松很多？
OPNsense 与双 WAN
我的计划是将 5G 网关插到 'ETH2' 上（也就是我 OPNsense 主机上的第三个以太网口；ETH0 接的是我的局域网，ETH1 接的是 Cable 调制解调器，ETH2 和 ETH3 空着——这些端口都是 2.5 Gbps 的）。
'ETH2' 对应的设备是 'igc2'，所以我登录了 OPNsense，在 Interfaces > Assignments 下，将新设备 'igc2' 分配并命名为 'WAN2'。
接着我在侧边栏点击 WAN2，并修改了以下设置：
Enable（勾选）
IPv4 Configuration Type: DHCP
点击 'Save'，然后点击顶部的 'Apply Changes'，接着进入 System > Gateways > Configuration，确认新的 WAN2 网关是否已经出现在那里。
（因为我不需要自动故障转移，所以我在这里没有设置任何特定的规则或监控，但如果你需要的话，可以自己研究一下怎么弄。）
进入 Firewall > NAT > Outbound，确保你已经设置了 'Automatic outbound NAT'。如果没有设置，你可能需要为 WAN2 接口添加一条规则。
故障转移
要实际切换到 WAN2：
访问 System > Gateways > Configuration
编辑 WAN2_DHCP，将 Priority 设置为 "1"（并确保它没有被 'Disabled'）
编辑 WAN_DHCP，将 Priority 设置为 "2"
点击 'Apply' 并等待几秒钟
我通常使用 curl icanhazip.com 或访问 fast.com 来确认我的电脑在任意时刻实际使用的是哪条网络连接。
要切回去，请将 WAN2_DHCP 设置为 "2"（或更高），将 WAN_DHCP 设置为 "1"（确保它没有被 'Disabled'），然后再次点击 'Apply'。

articles.title: Making an agile version of a Windows Runtime delegate in C++/WinRT, part 5
articles.titleZh: 在 C++/WinRT 中创建 Windows Runtime 委托的敏捷版本（第 5 部分）
articles.summary: 本系列文章的第 5 部分继续探讨如何在 C++/WinRT 中正确处理 Windows Runtime 委托的敏捷性。重点在于确保非敏捷委托以非敏捷的方式被使用，避免在跨线程调用时出现意外行为。文章深入分析了 COM 敏捷性与 Windows Runtime 组件交互时的底层机制。通过具体的代码示例，展示了如何安全地包装和调用非敏捷对象。结论是，理解并正确应用敏捷性规则是编写健壮的 C++/WinRT 应用程序的关键。
articles.summaryEn: Part 5 of this series continues to explore how to correctly handle the agility of Windows Runtime delegates in C++/WinRT. The focus is on ensuring that non-agile delegates are used non-agile-ly to avoid unexpected behavior during cross-thread calls. The article delves into the underlying mechanisms of COM agility when interacting with Windows Runtime components. Through specific code examples, it demonstrates how to safely wrap and invoke non-agile objects. The conclusion is that understanding and correctly applying agility rules is key to writing robust C++/WinRT applications.
articles.reason: 深入讲解了 C++/WinRT 中容易踩坑的委托敏捷性问题，是 Windows 平台底层开发者的必读参考资料。

blocks.text: So far, we have  handled the case of a non-marshalable delegate by wrapping it in a delegate that fails with CO_E_NOT_SUPPORTED if used in a manner that would require marshaling.
But we missed something.
Let’s look at it again.
While we copy and invoke the delegate only from its original context, we still destruct it from a possibly-wrong context.

This is a serious problem not just because the non-agile delegate might not be using thread-safe atomic instructions to manage its reference count, but even worse, if the release drops the reference count to zero, the delegate will destruct on the wrong thread, and that will probably create lots of problems.

We have to destruct the non-agile delegate in its original context. We can do this with a std::unique_ptr and a custom deleter. The std::unique_ptr handles all the move operations and the deleter cleans up the last pointer.

This stateful deleter remembers the context to use for final destruction. When it’s time to do the destruction, we switch into the target context via IContext­Callback::Context­Callback and take ownership of the raw pointer into a winrt::IUnknown. The destructor of the winrt::IUnknown will perform the release.
We can use this stateful deleter around the raw delegate pointer.
The first block gets a raw ABI pointer, either by moving it out of the inbound delegate if we can, else by copying it from the inbound delegate.
The second part wraps the raw ABI pointer inside a std::unique_ptr with our custom deleter, and the custom deleter makes sure that the Release of the original delegate happens in the correct context.
Are we done?
No!
More next time.
Author

Raymond has been involved in the evolution of Windows for more than 30 years. In 2003, he began a Web site known as The Old New Thing which has grown in popularity far beyond his wildest imagination, a development which still gives him the heebie-jeebies. The Web site spawned a book, coincidentally also titled The Old New Thing (Addison Wesley 2007). He occasionally appears on the Windows Dev Docs Twitter account to tell stories which convey no useful information.

translations: 到目前为止，我们处理不可封送委托的情况时，将其包装在另一个委托中，如果以需要封送的方式使用该委托，它就会失败并返回 CO_E_NOT_SUPPORTED。
但我们遗漏了一些东西。
让我们再看一下。
虽然我们仅在委托的原始上下文中复制和调用它，但我们仍然可能在错误的上下文中析构它。
这是一个严重的问题，不仅因为非敏捷委托可能没有使用线程安全的原子指令来管理其引用计数，更糟糕的是，如果释放操作将引用计数降为零，委托将在错误的线程上析构，这可能会引发许多问题。
我们必须在非敏捷委托的原始上下文中析构它。我们可以使用 std::unique_ptr 和自定义删除器来实现这一点。std::unique_ptr 处理所有的移动操作，而删除器负责清理最后一个指针。
这个有状态的删除器记住了用于最终析构的上下文。当需要执行析构时，我们通过 IContext­Callback::Context­Callback 切换到目标上下文，并将原始指针的所有权转移给一个 winrt::IUnknown。winrt::IUnknown 的析构函数将执行释放操作。
我们可以将这个有状态的删除器用于原始委托指针。
第一部分代码获取一个原始 ABI 指针，如果可能的话，将其从入站委托中移出，否则从入站委托中复制它。
第二部分使用我们的自定义删除器将原始 ABI 指针包装在 std::unique_ptr 中，自定义删除器确保原始委托的 Release 操作发生在正确的上下文中。
我们完成了吗？
没有！
下次再说更多。
作者

Raymond 参与了 Windows 的发展超过 30 年。2003 年，他创办了一个名为 The Old New Thing 的网站，其受欢迎程度远远超出了他最疯狂的想象，这一发展至今仍让他感到有些发怵。这个网站催生了一本书，巧合的是书名也叫《The Old New Thing》（Addison Wesley 2007 年出版）。他偶尔会出现在 Windows Dev Docs 的 Twitter 账号上，讲一些毫无实用信息的故事。

articles.title: ★ The Ads on Apple News Continue to Suck, but at Least There Are a Lot of Them
articles.titleZh: ★ Apple News 上的广告依然很烂，但至少数量很多
articles.summary: Apple 在广告服务方面的表现依然糟糕，他们在广告业务上并不擅长。这并不令人意外，因为广告服务的激励机制与 Apple 擅长的其他业务激励机制完全对立。Apple 的核心优势在于提供优质的硬件和隐私保护，而广告业务则要求牺牲用户体验来换取点击量。文章指出，尽管 Apple News 上的广告数量在增加，但其质量和相关性依然低下。结论是，Apple 试图在不破坏其品牌价值观的前提下做广告，注定无法在广告领域取得成功。
articles.summaryEn: Apple's performance in advertising services remains terrible; they are simply not good at advertising-based services. This is not surprising, as the incentives for advertising-based services are in direct opposition to the incentives for everything Apple is actually good at. Apple's core strengths lie in providing premium hardware and privacy protection, while advertising requires sacrificing user experience for clicks. The article points out that despite the increasing number of ads on Apple News, their quality and relevance remain low. The conclusion is that Apple's attempt to do advertising without compromising its brand values is doomed to fail in the advertising space.
articles.reason: 犀利剖析了 Apple 在广告业务上的内在矛盾，解释了为何这家硬件巨头始终无法做好广告服务。

blocks.text: Kirk McElhearn, back in February:

I use Apple News to keep up on topics that I don’t find in sources
I pay for (The Guardian and The New York Times). But there’s no
way I’m going to pay the exorbitant price Apple wants for Apple
News+ — £13 — because, while you get more publications, you
still get ads.

And those ads have gotten worse recently. Many if not most of them
look like and probably are scams. Here are a few examples from
Apple News today.

One of the ads he examined was, supposedly, from a small company going out of business because the proprietor — supposedly a straight-out-of-Central-Casting kind old woman — was retiring after 26 years. McElhearn looked up the domain name and it had only just been created last year, and was registered from a company in China.
Two years ago this very week, I wrote about Apple striking a deal with Taboola to sell ads for Apple News. In that post, I quoted Eric Seufert (of Mobile Dev Memo) posting on Threads:

Regarding Taboola’s partnership with Apple: I’ve seen people claim
that this is somehow hypocritical from a privacy perspective,
assuming that Taboola’s somewhat obnoxious, clickbait-style ads
must invasively target user profiles and browsing histories.

They don’t. They are targeted entirely contextually. That’s
the point.

Want brash, garish advertising plastered all over the web? Reject
ads personalization. Want relevant, informed advertising? Embrace
ads personalization.
Now quoting from myself in that same article:

If you told me that the ads in Apple News have been sold by
Taboola for the last few years, I’d have said, “Oh, that makes
sense.” Because the ads in Apple News — at least the ones I see — already look like chumbox Taboola ads. Even worse, they’re
incredibly repetitious. [...]

So while I don’t think it’s good news that Apple is partnering
with Taboola, I don’t expect it to make any discernible difference
in the ad quality or frequency. Maybe it will improve the variety?

Privacy is not the issue with Apple’s Taboola partnership, or Apple advertising in general. The issues are quality and user experience. I was correct that the partnership has made no discernible difference in ad quality or frequency. And it hasn’t made any improvement to variety either. Here’s a collection of ads I continue to see in Apple News — often with the same ad appearing 3–4 times in the same article, as I scroll. (I posted the same image in my recent article “John Ternus Should Reverse Apple’s Slide Down the Advertising Slippery Slope”, if you’re thinking it looks familiar.)

The ads I see in Apple News are not relevant or informed. And, to be clear, I have “Personalized Ads” turned on in Settings → Privacy & Security → Apple Advertising (which makes me wonder if turning that off might actually make the ads even worse). The ads shown in the App Store never seem contextually relevant to me. So I have no faith that the ads that Apple is supposedly on the cusp of serving in Apple Maps are going to be good.
Back in March I wrote:

I’m not going to prejudge the actual experience, and you shouldn’t
either. I also do not begrudge Apple for wanting to monetize
Maps. But if the addition of ads does make the Apple
Maps experience worse, why won’t Apple let us buy our way out of
seeing them? Netflix doesn’t force us to watch their
ads. YouTube Premium is arguably the best
bang-for-the-buck in the entire world of content subscriptions.
Why should Apple One subscribers still see these ads in
Apple Maps?

This to me is proof that Apple leadership is suffering from cognitive dissonance over their slide into advertising. They’re conflating cause and effect. The Apple brand stands for high-quality superior user experiences because the devices and software Apple makes traditionally deliver high-quality superior user experiences. The work Apple ships is what makes the brand what it is. But now they’re stricken with the mindset that it’s the Apple brand that makes something a high-quality superior experience. If it comes from Apple it must be great — that sort of thinking. The ads in Apple News and the App Store can’t be detrimental to the user experiences and at times even embarrassingly crude or downright scammy because Apple doesn’t ship things that are detrimental to the user experience or embarrassingly crude — and certainly never with even a whiff of scamminess.

My theory is that’s why Apple isn’t allowing users to buy our way out of the ads. When streaming services like Netflix let you pay more money for ad-free tiers, it’s an explicit acknowledgement that the experience with ads is worse. Apple doesn’t offer ad-free tiers for the App Store or (soon) Apple Maps1 because, I think, they can’t bring themselves to admit that by adding ads to these services they have made them worse. If you refuse to admit that the ads make these services worse, you also can’t admit that there’s a reason to offer an ad-free experience. So the thinking is something like “Apple always focuses on the user experience, and never deliberately makes the user experience worse. Therefore, if an Apple service shows ads, those ads are high quality and don’t detract from the quality of the product or the experience of using it. Therefore, there’s no reason to offer users a paid ad-free tier, because there’s no reason to want to avoid Apple’s ads.”

It’s a textbook case of Upton Sinclair’s famous adage: “It is difficult to get a man to understand something, when his salary depends upon his not understanding it.” The obvious truth is that Apple’s ads just plain suck. They are not good at advertising-based services. And it shouldn’t be surprising that they’re not good at advertising-based services, because the incentives for advertising-based services are in direct opposition to the incentives for everything Apple actually is good at. To wit: offering superior products worth paying a premium price for.

One can argue that an ad-free Apple Maps experience ought to be included with the price of the devices Apple sells (which, of course, has been true until now). It’s even easier to argue that the App Store ought to be ad-free for everyone, based on its exclusive role in software distribution and the 15–30 percent commission Apple takes on every transaction. But if Apple simply made the App Store and Apple Maps ad-free for users paying for iCloud+ or Apple One, I’d stop complaining. That would make it clear: the full Apple experience requires not just an Apple device, but an Apple subscription. But the way things stand now, that ad-free experience isn’t even available.

Apple News is different because the inclusion of ads is controlled by the publishers, not by Apple. If you read Daring Fireball on Apple News, for example, you don’t see their crummy chumbox ads, because I don’t participate in that system. Most of the cringe-inducing ads I see in Apple News are seemingly sold through Apple Ads, though, so I’m not arguing that Apple isn’t ultimately responsible for the Apple News reading experience. I’m saying they can’t just flip a switch and offer a paid-subscription no-ads Apple News experience without the agreement of every single participating publisher. The App Store and Apple Maps, however, are services under Apple’s complete control. Every ad shown in those apps is Apple’s choice to show. ↩︎

translations: Kirk McElhearn 在今年二月份曾写道：
我使用 Apple News 来关注那些我在付费订阅的来源（《卫报》和《纽约时报》）中看不到的话题。但我绝不会支付 Apple 为 Apple News+ 定下的高昂价格——13 英镑——因为，虽然你能看到更多出版物，但依然有广告。而且这些广告最近变得更糟了。其中很多甚至可以说是绝大多数，看起来像骗局，很可能就是骗局。以下是今天 Apple News 上的几个例子。
他查看的广告中，有一则据称来自一家即将倒闭的小公司，因为老板——一位仿佛从电影里走出来的慈祥老妇人——在经营26年后即将退休。McElhearn 查询了该域名，发现它去年才刚刚创建，并且是由一家中国公司注册的。
就在两年前的这一周，我写过关于 Apple 与 Taboola 达成协议，为 Apple News 销售广告的文章。在那篇文章中，我引用了 Eric Seufert（来自 Mobile Dev Memo）在 Threads 上的发帖：
关于 Taboola 与 Apple 的合作：我看到有人声称从隐私角度来看这有点虚伪，他们认为 Taboola 那些有些惹人厌的、标题党式的广告一定会侵入性地针对用户画像和浏览历史。其实并没有。它们完全是基于上下文进行定向投放的。这才是关键。想要网络上充斥着粗俗、花哨的广告吗？那就拒绝广告个性化。想要相关且经过筛选的广告吗？那就拥抱广告个性化。
现在引用我在同一篇文章中写的话：

如果你告诉我 Apple News 里的广告在过去几年里一直是由 Taboola 销售的，我会说：“哦，这说得通。”因为 Apple News 里的广告——至少我看到的那些——看起来已经像 Taboola 的诱饵盒广告了。更糟的是，它们重复得令人难以置信。[...] 所以，虽然我不认为 Apple 与 Taboola 合作是个好消息，但我也不指望它会对广告质量或频率产生任何明显的影响。也许它能增加广告的多样性？

隐私并不是 Apple 与 Taboola 合作或 Apple 广告业务普遍存在的问题。问题在于质量和用户体验。我说得对，这项合作并没有对广告质量或频率产生任何明显影响。它也没有改善广告的多样性。以下是我在 Apple News 中持续看到的一组广告——当我滚动屏幕时，同一篇文章中经常出现同一则广告3到4次。（如果你觉得眼熟，那是因为我在最近的文章《John Ternus 应该扭转 Apple 在广告滑坡上的下滑趋势》中发过同一张图片。）
我在 Apple News 中看到的广告既不相关也没有经过筛选。而且需要说明的是，我在“设置 → 隐私与安全性 → Apple 广告”中开启了“个性化广告”（这让我怀疑关掉它是否会让广告变得更糟）。App Store 中展示的广告对我来说似乎从来没有上下文相关性。因此，我对 Apple 据说即将在 Apple Maps 中投放的广告不抱任何期望。
回到三月份，我曾写道：
我不会预先评判实际体验，你也不应该。我也并不嫉妒 Apple 想要通过 Maps 变现。但如果增加广告确实让 Apple Maps 的体验变差，为什么 Apple 不让我们花钱免看这些广告呢？Netflix 并不强迫我们看他们的广告。YouTube Premium 可以说是整个内容订阅世界中性价比最高的选择。为什么 Apple One 的订阅者还要在 Apple Maps 中看到这些广告？

对我来说，这证明了苹果管理层在滑向广告业务的过程中正经历着认知失调。他们混淆了因果关系。苹果品牌代表着高质量、卓越的用户体验，因为苹果生产的设备和软件传统上确实能提供高质量、卓越的用户体验。苹果交付的产品成就了该品牌的地位。但现在他们却陷入了一种思维定势，认为是苹果品牌本身赋予了某物高质量、卓越的体验。“只要是苹果出品，必定是精品”——诸如此类的想法。他们觉得 Apple News 和 App Store 中的广告不可能损害用户体验，更不可能有时显得粗糙得令人尴尬，或者完全是骗局，因为苹果不会交付损害用户体验或粗糙得令人尴尬的东西——当然也绝不会带有任何欺诈的意味。

我的推论是，这就是为什么苹果不允许用户花钱免广告的原因。当像 Netflix 这样的流媒体服务让你多花钱购买无广告套餐时，这明确承认了有广告的体验更差。苹果没有为 App Store 或（即将推出的）Apple Maps 提供无广告套餐，我认为，是因为他们无法让自己承认，通过在这些服务中添加广告，他们已经让这些服务变差了。如果你拒绝承认广告让这些服务变差，你也就无法承认有理由提供无广告体验。所以他们的逻辑大概是这样的：“苹果始终专注于用户体验，从不刻意降低用户体验。因此，如果苹果的服务展示广告，这些广告也是高质量的，不会降低产品质量或使用体验。因此，没有理由向用户提供付费的无广告套餐，因为用户根本没有理由想要避开苹果的广告。”
这是厄普顿·辛克莱那句名言的教科书式案例：“当一个人的薪水取决于他不明白某件事时，就很难让他明白这件事。”显而易见的事实是，苹果的广告简直糟透了。他们不擅长基于广告的服务。他们不擅长基于广告的服务也不足为奇，因为基于广告的服务激励机制与苹果真正擅长的所有事情的激励机制截然相反。即：提供值得支付溢价的卓越产品。

人们可以争辩说，无广告的 Apple Maps 体验本应包含在苹果出售的设备价格中（当然，到目前为止确实如此）。基于 App Store 在软件分发中的独家角色以及苹果从每笔交易中抽取的 15% 到 30% 的佣金，主张 App Store 应该对所有人无广告就更容易说得通了。但如果苹果仅仅为支付 iCloud+ 或 Apple One 的用户提供无广告的 App Store 和 Apple Maps，我就会停止抱怨。这将明确一点：完整的苹果体验不仅需要苹果设备，还需要苹果的订阅服务。但就目前的情况而言，那种无广告的体验甚至根本无法获得。

Apple News 有所不同，因为广告的投放是由出版商控制的，而非 Apple。例如，如果你在 Apple News 上阅读 Daring Fireball，你就看不到那些低劣的 chumbox 广告，因为我不参与那套系统。不过，我在 Apple News 上看到的大多数令人尴尬的广告似乎都是通过 Apple Ads 售出的，所以我并不是说 Apple 对 Apple News 的阅读体验没有最终责任。我的意思是，如果没有每一个参与出版商的同意，他们不能简单地一按开关就提供无广告的 Apple News 付费订阅体验。然而，App Store 和 Apple Maps 是完全由 Apple 掌控的服务。在这些应用中展示的每一条广告都是 Apple 自己的选择。 ↩︎

articles.title: Podcast Notes: Ed Catmull on David Senra
articles.titleZh: 播客笔记：Ed Catmull 接受 David Senra 采访
articles.summary: 皮克斯联合创始人兼迪士尼动画前总裁 Ed Catmull 在 David Senra 播客中分享了他的管理理念。他认为自己的核心工作是“为团队群体建立正确的动态”。访谈内容涉及如何营造有利于创造力的团队环境。作者还推荐了 Catmull 的著作《创新公司》。
articles.summaryEn: Ed Catmull, co-founder of Pixar and former president of Disney Animation, shared his management philosophy on the David Senra podcast. He considered his core job to be getting the dynamics right for groups of people. The interview covers how to foster a team environment conducive to creativity. The author also recommends reading Catmull's book, Creativity, Inc.
articles.reason: 了解皮克斯联合创始人如何通过管理团队动态来激发创造力。

blocks.text: Ed Catmull, co-founder of Pixar and former president of Disney Animation, was on the David Senra podcast and I quite enjoyed the interview.
(If you like the interview, you should read his book.)
Ed talks about what he considered his job to be: get the dynamics right for groups of people working together.

To do this, he would pull people out of meetings, make groups smaller, make them bigger, just constantly work on fine-tuning getting the right people together at the right time with the right feedback (without ego).
Granted he didn’t always do it, but that was his goal. He says:

This is so important to get [these group dynamics right] because this is what our product is based on: getting this group of people to work well together. So paying attention to the dynamics of the room is the job. They’re the ones making the movies. I’m not making the movie. I’m just trying to get them to work well together.
When Steve Jobs came to Ed and essentially said, “We’re gonna bet everything at Pixar on Toy Story, and the same week that Toy Story is released in theaters we’re gonna IPO.” What did Ed think?
I thought it was crazy [laugh] I’ve learned a lot in this process. He was right.
I love this frank exchange and Ed’s ability to go from “I thought he was crazy” to “I learned”.

In a creative endeavor, where so many earlier iterations suck, how do you gauge whether you should keep going? Because to keep going can make you seem a tad crazy, e.g. “This sucks — let’s keep going!”
So how do you know whether you should keep investing in it? Ed’s answer:

What’s your basis for proceeding? For me, the basis was: what’s the spirit of the team? Because we all know it [sucks] but if they’re all working together — they’re laughing, and [doing things] together — then you say, “Let’s keep going. Let’s keep trying to solve it.”
I love this. He didn’t say, “You open a spreadsheet and do a cost analysis.” He said he looks at the spirit of the people working on it.
It really backs up what he said his job is: find and help groups of people work together. His attitude seems to be: a group of people with the right dynamics can solve anything.
Ed talks about Pixar’s willingness to take on hard problems because they believed a hard problem led to better outcomes (because few others were willing to do the hard work):

A hard problem is more likely to lead to an interesting film. If it’s easy, then it’s more derivative.
You know how to write a script, you know what the three-act structure is, you know all these elements of storytelling, and you put together all the pieces and you got a story. Is it a great story? Is it emotional? Sometimes yes, sometimes no […]
It’s fairly easy to come up with something that is mediocre — and it’s cheaper too.
If you take on hard things then you need to spend more time trying to figure out how to be different in what you’re doing. So if you take on a hard problem and you just keep pushing at it, then the fact that it was hard is what is going to make it different.
Stated again for emphasis: “the fact that it was hard is what is going to make it different”.
And it’s the execution that’s hard, not having the idea:

If you’re going to make a movie about a rat that likes to cook, that is not a slam dunk.
A lot of people want to keep their projects secret, but this is one where you could tell everybody: “We’re going to make a movie about a rat that cooks!”

His point being: nobody can steal that idea and make it good. Execution is everything there. And if you look at it and say, “Well that’s too hard. How could you make a film about a rat that likes to cook?” You’re skirting the hard work, which is exactly what is going to make you different.
Don’t skirt the hard thing. If you do something that’s hard, that’s the differentiation.
Lastly: I love Ed’s perspective on mission statements:
The reason [we never had a mission statement] is because a mission statement is an answer, when typically we should always be asking questions, like “What are we doing?”

His point being: if somebody asks “What are we doing?” and you immediately go back to the mission statement and say, “Oh, well we’re doing this” that’s not good. It’s better to always be questioning. “Are we doing the right thing? Are we going in the right direction?” You should always be wrestling with those questions.

translations: Ed Catmull，Pixar 联合创始人兼 Disney Animation 前总裁，参加了 David Senra 的播客节目，我非常喜欢这期访谈。
（如果你喜欢这期访谈，你应该去读读他的书。）
Ed 谈到了他认为自己的工作是什么：让团队协作的互动状态保持良好。
为此，他会把人从会议中拉出来，缩小团队规模，或者扩大团队规模，不断微调，确保在对的时间让对的人聚在一起，并给予恰当的反馈（不带个人自负）。
诚然，他并不总是能做到，但那是他的目标。他说：
把[团队互动调整好]非常重要，因为这是我们的产品的基础：让这群人很好地协同工作。所以，关注会议室里的互动状态就是我的工作。电影是他们拍的。我不是在拍电影。我只是努力让他们更好地合作。
当 Steve Jobs 找到 Ed 并明确表示：“我们要把 Pixar 的一切都押在《Toy Story》上，并且在《Toy Story》上映的同一周，我们要进行 IPO。” Ed 当时是怎么想的？
我觉得这太疯狂了 [笑]。在这个过程中我学到了很多。他是对的。
我很喜欢这种坦诚的交流，以及 Ed 从“我觉得他疯了”转变为“我学到了”的能力。
在创意工作中，早期的许多迭代都很糟糕，你如何判断是否应该继续下去？因为继续下去可能会让你显得有点疯狂，比如“这太烂了——我们继续吧！”
那么，你怎么知道是否应该继续投入呢？Ed 的回答是：
你继续下去的依据是什么？对我来说，依据是：团队的精神状态如何？因为我们都知道它[很烂]，但如果他们都在协同工作——他们有说有笑，一起[做事]——那么你就会说，“我们继续吧。我们继续尝试解决它。”
我很喜欢这个回答。他没有说，“你打开电子表格做个成本分析。”他说他看重的是参与其中的人的精神状态。
这确实印证了他所说的自己的工作：寻找并帮助团队协同工作。他的态度似乎是：一个互动状态良好的团队可以解决任何问题。
Ed 谈到了 Pixar 愿意挑战难题，因为他们相信难题能带来更好的结果（因为很少有人愿意去做这种艰难的工作）：

难题更有可能成就一部有趣的电影。如果很容易，那它就更具衍生性。
你知道怎么写剧本，你知道三幕剧结构是什么，你知道讲故事的这些所有元素，你把所有碎片拼凑起来，就得到了一个故事。它是一个伟大的故事吗？它有情感吗？有时有，有时没有 […]
弄出平庸的东西相当容易——而且成本也更低。
如果你挑战艰难的事情，那么你需要花更多时间去弄清楚如何让你所做的事情与众不同。所以，如果你接手一个难题并不断推进，那么它之所以困难，正是它将与众不同的原因。
再次强调：“它之所以困难，正是它将与众不同的原因”。
而且困难在于执行，而不是产生想法：

如果你要拍一部关于一只喜欢做饭的老鼠的电影，那并不是稳操胜券的。
很多人想对自己的项目保密，但这个项目你可以告诉所有人：“我们要拍一部关于一只会做饭的老鼠的电影！”
他的观点是：没人能偷走那个创意并把它做好。执行力才是关键所在。如果你看着它说：“嗯，这太难了。怎么能拍一部关于一只喜欢做饭的老鼠的电影呢？”你就是在逃避困难的工作，而这恰恰是让你与众不同的地方。
不要逃避困难的事情。如果你做的事情很难，那就是差异化。
最后：我很喜欢 Ed 对使命宣言的看法：
[我们从未有过使命宣言的]原因在于，使命宣言是一个答案，而通常我们应该始终在提出问题，比如“我们在做什么？”
他的观点是：如果有人问“我们在做什么？”而你立刻搬出使命宣言说：“哦，我们在做这个”，那是不好的。最好始终保持质疑。“我们做的事情对吗？我们的方向正确吗？”你应该始终在这些问题上反复斟酌。

articles.title: Sixers Sign LeBron James
articles.summary: 勒布朗·詹姆斯宣布加盟费城76人队，该队夺得NBA总冠军的赔率随即从20-1降至10-1。詹姆斯在社交媒体上表示，此次签约不为金钱或家庭，而是为了继续牺牲、努力和竞争，以追求再次夺冠的感觉。他相信自己能帮助76人队成为冠军球队。
articles.summaryEn: LeBron James announced his signing with the Philadelphia 76ers, causing their NBA championship betting odds to drop from 20-1 to 10-1. James stated on social media that this decision was not about money or family, but about continuing to sacrifice, work, and compete for another championship. He believes he can help make the 76ers a championship team.

What you should know
LeBron James is signing a two-year deal with the Sixers, according to ESPN's Shams Charania.
The 41-year-old James, the NBA's all-time leading scorer, is entering his 24th season. A future Hall of Famer and four-time NBA champion, James spent the last eight seasons with the Lakers.
Earlier this month, the Sixers acquired Jaylen Brown from the Celtics in exchange for Paul George and four draft picks.
The Sixers' projected starting lineup now includes James, Brown, Tyrese Maxey, VJ Edgecombe, and Joel Embiid.
How did LeBron land in Philly? We've been tracking all the twists and turns — and hints — along the way.

Sixers president of basketball operations Mike Gansey has a history with James. They first crossed paths as Ohio high school basketball players and later when Gansey was an executive with the Cavaliers.

Sielski: LeBron's arrival changes everything

Steph Curry changed the way basketball was played and the way boys and girls around the world wanted to play it, and among the fraternity of NBA players themselves, Kobe Bryant was more respected and feared, for his preparation and cutthroat competitiveness. But LeBron James has been greater longer than any other player in the sport (with the possible exception of Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, if you count his Lew Alcindor/UCLA years).

Set aside, if possible, the four NBA championships and the 10 Finals appearances and the league’s career scoring record and the three Olympic gold medals and the other records he has set. His choreographed announcement in 2010 that he was leaving the Cleveland Cavaliers for the Miami Heat was the 21st century’s answer to the revelation that Kristin Shepard had pumped two bullets into J.R. Ewing’s belly. It changed everything about the power that elite players held over their respective teams because it showed elite players that they held power over their respective teams. Pro sports hasn’t been the same.

Finding an athlete comparable to James in popularity and influence is difficult enough, let alone one who arrived in Philadelphia during the middle stage or latter half of his career, after he had established his galactic superstardom. Wilt Chamberlain already had been a high school phenom here when the Warriors made him a territorial pick in the 1959 NBA draft. Julius Erving was the “Babe Ruth of basketball” — at least, that’s how Sixers general manager Pat Williams described him in trying to persuade owner Fitz Dixon to cough up the money to acquire Dr. J. But Erving had spent six years in the relative obscurity of the ABA; telling someone you had seen him play for the Virginia Squires or New York Nets, whether in person or on TV, was akin to claiming you had spotted a Sasquatch.

据 ESPN 的 Shams Charania 报道，勒布朗·詹姆斯正在与 76 人队签下一份为期两年的合同。
41 岁的詹姆斯是 NBA 历史总得分王，即将迎来他的第 24 个赛季。作为未来的名人堂成员和四届 NBA 总冠军，詹姆斯过去八个赛季都在湖人队效力。
本月早些时候，76 人队从凯尔特人队交易来了杰伦·布朗，换走了保罗·乔治和四个选秀权。
76 人队预计的首发阵容现在包括詹姆斯、布朗、泰瑞斯·马克西、VJ Edgecombe 和乔尔·恩比德。
勒布朗是如何落脚费城的？我们一直在追踪这一路上的所有波折与暗示。
76 人队篮球运营总裁迈克·甘西与詹姆斯有着一段渊源。他们最初是在俄亥俄州的高中篮球赛场上相识的，后来在甘西担任骑士队高管时再次相遇。

勒布朗解释了他为什么选择76人队
在勒布朗·詹姆斯计划与76人队签下两年合同的消息传出后不久，这位未来的名人堂球员在社交媒体上解释了他最新的决定。以下是全文：
“当赛季结束时，我以为我的职业生涯已经结束了。我还没准备好宣布这件事，我知道我需要一些时间来做真正的决定，但我相当确信我已经打完了最后一场比赛。在上次新闻发布会上我很坦诚，我说我需要审视自己，决定是否依然热爱这项运动。我依然真心热爱这项运动，而且我还有更多能量可以奉献。”
“过去的几周真的很特别。我从未有过这种毫无头绪、能真正花时间去思考的经历。我和所有我爱的人度过了不可思议的几个月，试图理清这一切。这是我的最终决定。我不为钱，也不为家人。到了这个阶段，我究竟是为了什么而打球？”
6小时前
Sielski：勒布朗的到来改变了一切
斯蒂芬·库里改变了篮球的打法，也改变了全世界男孩女孩们渴望打球的方式；而在NBA球员的圈子里，科比·布莱恩特因其备战态度和残酷的竞争力而更受尊重与敬畏。但勒布朗·詹姆斯在这项运动中保持伟大的时间比任何其他球员都要长（如果把卡里姆·阿卜杜勒-贾巴尔的刘易斯·阿尔辛多/UCLA时期算在内，他可能是唯一的例外）。
如果可能的话，暂且抛开那四个NBA总冠军、十次打进总决赛、联盟历史总得分纪录、三枚奥运金牌以及他所创造的其他纪录。他在2010年精心策划的离开克利夫兰骑士队转投迈阿密热火队的声明，堪称21世纪版的“克里斯汀·谢泼德向J.R.尤因腹部连开两枪”的惊天大揭秘。它彻底改变了精英球员对各自球队所拥有的权力格局，因为它让精英球员意识到，他们能够掌控各自的球队。职业体育从此被彻底改变。

找到一位在人气和影响力上能与詹姆斯相提并论的运动员已经够难了，更不用说是一位在确立了自己超级巨星地位后，在职业生涯中后期来到费城的球员了。威尔特·张伯伦在这里早就是高中篮球奇才了，勇士队在1959年NBA选秀中将其作为属地球员选中。朱利叶斯·欧文是“篮球界的贝比·鲁斯”——至少，76人队总经理帕特·威廉姆斯在试图说服老板菲茨·迪克森掏钱引进“J博士”时是这么形容他的。但欧文曾在ABA联盟默默无闻地度过了六年；告诉别人你曾看过他为弗吉尼亚绅士队或纽约篮网队打球，无论是现场还是电视转播，都无异于声称你目击了大脚怪。
6小时前
詹姆斯何时迎来76人队首秀？
目前，我们仍在等待NBA公布76人队2026-27赛季的完整赛程，但周一已经有一些季前赛消息流出，包括10月10日（客场，晚上8点）和10月16日（主场，晚上7点）对阵波士顿凯尔特人队的两场比赛。这两场比赛很可能会在NBC Sports Philadelphia播出，但也有可能被提升至全国电视网转播。
而这还是假设詹姆斯会出战季前赛的情况。
41岁的詹姆斯可能会选择等到常规赛揭幕战才迎来76人队首秀，尽管近年来他都有参加季前赛，但上赛季除外，当时他因坐骨神经痛缺席了常规赛前14场比赛。
—— 马特·穆林

迈克·甘西最初以球员身份赢得了詹姆斯的尊重
到现在你可能已经看过那张照片了。它拍摄于2000年，登上了《克利夫兰老实人报》体育版头版。十名来自俄亥俄州东北部的高中篮球运动员穿着各自的球衣并肩站立。
这群人被教练和体育主管评选为该地区最优秀的球员。左边是马弗里克·卡特和切斯特·梅森（“喷气机切特”）。布莱恩·斯威夫特更靠近中间，旁边是迈克·帕特里克。
但真正引起所有人注意的是最右边：来自奥尔姆斯特德福尔斯高中的迈克·甘西——未来的76人队篮球运营总裁，旁边是来自圣文森特-圣玛丽高中的勒布朗·詹姆斯——未来的名人堂球员。

从里奇·保罗白板上泰瑞斯·马克西名字旁边的星号，到勒布朗·詹姆斯说他想“相信过程”——再到史蒂夫·甘西疯传的照片，以及泰瑞斯·哈利伯顿问詹姆斯这是否是他的第76个赛季——从来不乏指向“国王詹姆斯”最终与76人队签约的彩蛋。

articles.title: Becoming Skilled at Making Documents
articles.summary: 商业环境中使用的绝大多数文档质量堪忧，演示文稿和备忘录往往让人难以理解，甚至更多地暴露了制作过程而非传达信息。作者 Anil Dash 长期以来对此感到沮丧，并曾撰写《Make Better Documents》一文。本文进一步探讨了如何通过提升技能来制作更清晰、更有效的商业文档。
articles.summaryEn: The vast majority of business documents are of poor quality, with presentations and memos that are inscrutable and reveal more about their creation process than their intended message. Author Anil Dash expresses his long-standing frustration with this issue and references his previous post, Make Better Documents. This article further explores how to develop the skills needed to create clearer and more effective business documents.
articles.reason: 获取改善日常商业文档质量的具体建议，提升职场沟通效率。

blocks.text: The vast majority of the documents people use to do business are really quite poor. Presentations that make your eyes glaze over, memos that are inscrutable or unclear, and all kinds of artifacts that say more about how they were created than whatever message they were ostensibly trying to communicate. It's been one of my great frustrations for years, and a big part of why I wrote Make Better Documents a while ago. That post captured a list of the suggestions I've been giving people for years on how to make better, more effective documents that can actually do work for you, instead of fighting at cross purposes to your larger goals.

To my great surprise, that list of suggestions on how to make better documents got a pretty huge response, and a lot of people told me they found it really helpful. So now, I've created a Better Documents skills.md file for people who use LLM tools like Claude to help assist them in creating business documents, to prompt their AI tools to make better documents by default.

If you're not familiar, agent skills are simple text files that describe new capabilities or processes that LLMs can take advantage of when carrying out tasks. (They're Markdown files — more proof of how Markdown is taking over the world!) The way this skill works is that it's distilled the broad principles I outlined in that post into a series of 5 tests, covering areas like whether you've properly considered your target audience, whether the overall structure is correct, if you've overdone things with your formatting, and if things are named clearly, and then either generates a new file that follows those rules, or reviews an existing document to make sure it is obeying best practices.

It's nothing too fancy, but I've been using it for a while, and shared it with a few friends, and people have told me they found it handy and it's improved some of their routine documents. I'm especially glad that people have found it useful even if they're the kind of folks who would never let an LLM generate a document on their behalf, but do think software tools are useful for things like spell check or grammar check. I see this as being a tool in that kind of category.

If you're familiar with skills, the install process is really simple and works just like any other skill. This skill is totally free and open source (if you have improvements, send along a pull request on GitHub, or if you're not a coder type, just email me or hit me up on social media and let me know what fixes/suggestions you've got), so there are no encumbrances or restrictions on its use. I am curious if it's useful to people, especially if you find it handy to use more broadly at a company, so don't be shy to get in touch if you find it valuable.
Here's to us all enduring fewer terrible presentations!

translations: 人们日常用于商业活动的大多数文档质量实在堪忧。那些让人看得昏昏欲睡的演示文稿、晦涩难懂的备忘录，以及各种只顾展示制作过程却偏离了本应传达信息的文件。多年来这一直让我感到十分沮丧，也是我前段时间写下《Make Better Documents》一文的重要原因。那篇文章总结了我多年来给人们的一系列建议，指导他们如何制作出更好、更有效的文档，让文档真正为你所用，而不是与你的宏大目标背道而驰。
令我惊讶的是，那份关于如何制作更好文档的建议清单引起了巨大的反响，很多人告诉我他们觉得这非常有帮助。因此，我现在为使用 Claude 等 LLM 工具辅助创建商业文档的用户创建了一个 Better Documents skills.md 文件，以提示他们的 AI 工具默认生成更好的文档。

如果你不熟悉的话，agent skills 是一些简单的文本文件，用于描述 LLM 在执行任务时可以利用的新功能或流程。（它们是 Markdown 文件——这再次证明了 Markdown 正在接管世界！）这项技能的工作原理是，将我在那篇文章中概述的宽泛原则提炼为 5 项测试，涵盖你是否充分考虑了目标受众、整体结构是否正确、格式是否过度修饰、命名是否清晰等方面，然后要么生成一个遵循这些规则的新文件，要么审查现有文档以确保其符合最佳实践。
它并没有什么花哨的功能，但我已经用了一段时间，并分享给了几个朋友，大家都说它很方便，而且改善了一些日常文档。让我特别高兴的是，即使是那些绝不会让 LLM 代为生成文档、但认为软件工具在拼写检查或语法检查方面很有用的人，也觉得它很有帮助。我认为它就是属于那一类工具。

如果你熟悉 skills，安装过程非常简单，就像安装任何其他 skill 一样。这项技能完全免费且开源（如果你有改进建议，可以在 GitHub 上提交 pull request；如果你不是程序员，只需给我发电子邮件或在社交媒体上联系我，告诉我你的修改/建议即可），因此在使用上没有任何负担或限制。我很好奇它是否对大家有用，特别是如果你觉得在公司内部更广泛地使用它很方便，如果你觉得它有价值，请不要害羞，随时与我联系。
愿我们都能少忍受一些糟糕的演示文稿！
