blocks.text: The following is a transcript of episode 214 of Green Squares, a podcast about building in public and staying green. It has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Transcription by OpenClaw-4.2.

TYLER: Welcome back to Green Squares, I’m Tyler. Longtime listeners know I came up doing Proof of Work, rest in peace, and one thing I carried over from that show is a belief that the most interesting people in tech are the ones holding up infrastructure you’ve never heard of. You’ve all seen the xkcd. The whole internet, balanced on one project, maintained by some guy in Nebraska. Today we’ve got that guy. Erin Marsh maintains libcapstan, the reference implementation of the Capstan protocol. If you’ve ever resumed a download, synced a device, or updated an app on a bad connection, you’ve run her code. Erin, welcome to the show.
ERIN: Thanks for having me.
TYLER: So let’s do the numbers, because they’re wild. Eighty million downloads a month. Something like forty thousand packages depend on you. And it’s basically just you?
ERIN: There were three of us until 2023. One co-maintainer left when he had kids. The other stepped back last year, he has a farm now. So mostly me, yes.
TYLER: Incredible. And you’re calling in from New Zealand, which means it’s currently, what,
ERIN: Six in the morning.
TYLER: The dedication. OK, origin story. How does one person end up maintaining a foundational protocol library?

ERIN: I reported some bugs in it. This was 2019, we used it at work, and the resume logic could corrupt files on flaky connections. I sent a report with a reproduction and a suggested fix, and the maintainer at the time said this was exactly the kind of energy the project needed, and gave me commit access. About a month later I got a repository transfer invitation. I accepted it. It seemed like the polite thing to do.
TYLER: He saw something in you.
ERIN: He’d moved onto a sailboat.

TYLER: Love that for him. So let’s get into the AI of it all, because that’s really why I wanted you on. You’re one person supporting this enormous surface area. The new tooling has to be a huge unlock, right? Are you using any of the agents day to day?
ERIN: I’ve tried things. I had a Copilot subscription for a while.
TYLER: How was it?

ERIN: Mixed. The codebase is C from 2011, which the tooling has opinions about. In April I asked it to add a bounds check, and it reformatted the file from tabs to spaces on the way through. The linter flagged that, so it saw the failure and reformatted back to tabs. That introduced trailing whitespace, which the linter also flags. It went around that loop until my included tokens ran out. Nothing came back. I wrote the bounds check myself.
TYLER: Growing pains. But the trajectory is what excites me. What about the contribution side? Because the dream is that agents pick up the long tail, right, the issues no human wants to do.

ERIN: We get a lot of agent contributions now. Last month it was around sixty pull requests a week. They’re polite, well formatted, and they come with tests. Most of them do something we don’t want. There’s an issue from 2016 about symlink handling where we’ve explained our position maybe two hundred times, and the agents find that issue and fix it, and each one has to be told separately. We added an AGENTS.md at the root of the repo asking automated contributors to check the tracker before opening anything. It’s now the most edited file in the repository. They send fixes for it. One of the typos was real, so I merged that one.
TYLER: Sixty a week, though. Some of that has to be gold.

ERIN: Three were useful this year. One was excellent, actually, a race in the retry logic that none of us had caught in a decade. I’d like to thank whoever ran that agent, but the account was already deleted.
TYLER: So what would actually move the needle for you? If the people building these tools are listening, and they do listen, what do you want the agents doing?
ERIN: Review is the bottleneck, not code. What I’d really love is

TYLER: Hold that thought, because we have to pay some bills. This episode of Green Squares is brought to you by Foreman. You know the feeling. It’s Sunday night, your contribution graph has a gap, and the side project isn’t going to build itself. Foreman is the autonomous engineer that ships while you sleep. Point it at any repository, yours or anyone’s, and Foreman finds the open issues, writes the fix, opens the pull request, and replies to review comments in your voice until it gets merged. Foreman users open an average of 340 pull requests a month across more than two thousand open source projects. Go to tryforeman.dev/green for twenty percent off your first three months. Foreman. Keep shipping. And we’re back. Erin, you were saying, what would help?
ERIN: I don’t remember where I was going with that.
TYLER: It’ll come back to you. Let’s talk security, because libcapstan is in everything, and everything means exposure. Walk me through what happens when a report comes in.

ERIN: We get about ten a month now, up from one or two a few years ago. Most are automated, a scanner finding, wrapped in a model-written report. The reports are long and very confident, and roughly one in fifteen describes a real problem. So the actual work is verification, and that part stays with me, because it’s the one thing you have to get right.
TYLER: See, this feels like exactly what frontier models are for. Have you tried throwing AI at the verification itself?
ERIN: I did, last November. I set up an agent to take each incoming report, build the affected version, and try to reproduce the exploit in a sandbox. It worked well for two weeks.
TYLER: And then?

ERIN: The account was banned. Reproducing an exploit looks the same as developing one from the provider’s side. I appealed, and the appeal form asks you to describe what you were doing, and describing it triggered the same filter. So the appeal got me banned as well.
TYLER: [laughs] There’s got to be a path though. A research tier, something.
ERIN: There’s a form. It asks for your institution.
TYLER: What about the human researchers? The security community catches so much these days, that relationship has to be valuable.

ERIN: The individuals are mostly great. The companies are harder. In February a vendor found a real issue in our header parsing, a bad one, and their analysis was good. They also filed it directly on the public issue tracker, proof of concept included, on a Tuesday. The writeup was scheduled for their blog that Wednesday, and their policy is ninety days or publication, whichever comes first. The vulnerability had a name and a logo before I finished reading the report. There was a countdown clock. I shipped the fix in twenty-six hours, and their post described that as an encouraging response from a historically under-resourced project. Then their sales team emailed companies that depend on us, offering a hardened version of libcapstan.
TYLER: Hardened how?
ERIN: As far as I can tell it’s our releases with my security patches applied. They’re on the embargo list, so they can ship my fix a few days before I do.
TYLER: I want to get to sustainability, but first, flip side. You’re a downstream consumer too. You have your own dependency tree. What does that look like from where you sit?

ERIN: We have four dependencies. We had six. Last year I audited them and found problems in one, a checksum library, and reported everything upstream with patches. The maintainer thanked me, merged all of it, and two weeks later there was a transfer invitation waiting. I knew what it was this time. We depend on the library, so.
TYLER: Again?
ERIN: It’s the second time it’s happened. I now maintain a good chunk of my own dependency tree. I’ve stopped reporting bugs upstream.
TYLER: And you said six down to four.

ERIN: The other one we removed was a small library we’d depended on since 2014 for one function, so I inlined the function. And then I got a long email from its maintainer, because there’s a company called WaveRiser that pays maintainers based on their position in dependency trees. Being removed from ours dropped him under some threshold, and he lost about four hundred dollars a month. He was apologetic about it. He offered me a hundred and fifty a month to add it back.
TYLER: Did you take it?
ERIN: It would have been the project’s largest source of income.

TYLER: OK, that is actually a perfect segue, because, full disclosure, listeners already know this. This episode is also sponsored by WaveRiser. If your business runs on open source, and it does, WaveRiser makes sure the maintainers behind your stack are taken care of. Their dependency intelligence engine maps every package in your tree, scores each one for criticality, and routes funding automatically to the projects that matter most. No invoices, no phone calls with maintainers, no overhead. Enterprise plans start at ninety-nine dollars a seat. WaveRiser, the supply chain, sustained. And Erin, you must be glad they exist, honestly.
ERIN: They’ve never contacted me.
TYLER: Well, it’s automatic. That’s the whole product. It routes to the projects that matter most.
ERIN: Yes.
TYLER: While we’re on money. You know my history, I spent three years in web3, and I’m curious whether any of that ever reached you. Token models for funding infrastructure, that whole thesis.

ERIN: It reached me once. In 2022 someone launched CapstanCoin. I learned about it eight months later, from the emails, because it had collapsed and the treasury had been drained, and some of the holders found my address in the git log. The website had a roadmap with my name on it. There was a whitepaper citing my commit history as proof of ongoing development, which I suppose it was. About two million dollars went through it, none of it to me, and for a while I was getting demands for refunds. One man emailed me for a year. He was always polite. He’d retired on the strength of it.
TYLER: Early days. The space matured a lot after that, though. Honestly the part that went mainstream is prediction markets. Does that world ever touch yours?

ERIN: There’s a market on whether I’ll step down before the end of the year. I found out about it when a stranger messaged me asking if I could hold on until January, because of the resolution date. And during the February disclosure there was one on how fast we’d patch. The vendor traded it before their post went out.

TYLER: Efficient markets. OK, I want to ask about capstan-rs, because I know it’s a sensitive one. For listeners: last year a developer rewrote libcapstan in Rust over a weekend, capstan-rs, blazingly fast resumable transfers, that was the tagline, and it hit forty thousand stars in a month. Which, Erin, I checked, is ten times your stars. In a month. What did that feel like?
ERIN: The benchmarks measured throughput on a warm cache with resume disabled. Resume is the hard part. It’s all edge cases, which is why the library exists. Rewrites get to skip that.
TYLER: Very gracious.
ERIN: He was hired by the company behind OpenClaw off the back of it, and the repository was archived in March. We still get issues asking when libcapstan is migrating to it.
TYLER: And then there’s the fork. I debated even bringing this up.

ERIN: It’s fine. Earlier this year we started blocking OpenClaw agents from the repo, because we kept getting pull requests that added the agent’s operator to the copyright headers. So we blocked the traffic, and about six weeks later OpenClaw announced a clean-room implementation of the Capstan protocol, written, according to the announcement, without reference to our code.
TYLER: Competition keeps everyone sharp though, right?

ERIN: It reproduces a bug we’ve had open since 2021. Byte for byte, the same wrong output. We have a regression test for it, named after the issue number, and their test suite has a test with the same name that asserts the wrong output is correct. I filed an issue about it. Their tracker has about five thousand open, mostly from other agents, and the triage bot answers them in order. It hasn’t got to mine yet.

TYLER: OK, sustainability, properly this time. Because I hear all of this and I think, this is a funding problem, and there is more money pointed at open source than ever. Foundations, the sovereign tech funds, all of it. Have you gone after any?

ERIN: I applied for a grant last year. The protocol is being extended for multipath, and libcapstan is the reference implementation, so whatever we ship becomes the standard in practice. I asked for six months of funding to do the design work properly, with a spec, instead of at eleven at night.
TYLER: Slam dunk, surely.

ERIN: Declined. The criteria weight participation in the standards process, and I’ve never been able to join the working group. The working group meets on a video platform that doesn’t work in Firefox, and I use Firefox. I raised it, and the group agreed it was a problem, and raised it with the platform, and the platform’s position is that Firefox is not a supported enterprise browser. So on paper I have no standards experience. The reviewers said the implementation work was impressive, but that implementation is not participation.
TYLER: Couldn’t you just use Chrome for the calls?
ERIN: I’ve considered it.
TYLER: All right, closing questions, we do these with every guest. Five years from now, where’s libcapstan?
ERIN: Still underneath everything, I expect. It’s very hard to remove.
TYLER: And where are you?
ERIN: My old co-maintainer’s farm is doing well. Sixty goats now, and the cheese has a waiting list. I joined it.
TYLER: [laughs] Amazing. Erin, this was fantastic. Where do people go to support the project?
ERIN: There’s a sponsors link in the readme.

TYLER: Perfect, we’ll put it in the show notes. And before we go, a quick one from our friends at AgentDays, September 14th to 16th in Austin. Conference season is rough when you’re heads down, so this year, register your agents and they attend for you. Every talk published as structured context, and a networking layer where your agents take meetings while you sleep. Erin, this might be one for you, honestly.
ERIN: Mm.

TYLER: Agent passes start at forty-nine dollars, humans get in free with any agent pass, code SQUARES for ten percent off. And you can support this show at patreon.com/greensquares, we just crossed four thousand patrons, which is very cool of you all. That’s the episode. If you got value out of this one, the single best thing you can do is share it with a friend. Next week I sit down with the founder of Foreman to talk about the future of autonomous contribution. Until then. Keep shipping.

translations: 以下是《Green Squares》第214期的文字记录，这是一档关于公开构建和保持环保的播客。为了篇幅和清晰度，内容经过了轻微编辑。由 OpenClaw-4.2 转录。

TYLER：欢迎回到《Green Squares》，我是 Tyler。老听众都知道我是做 Proof of Work 起家的，愿它安息，我从那档节目里保留下来的一点是：科技界最有趣的人，往往是那些支撑着你闻所未闻的基础设施的人。你们都看过那幅 xkcd 漫画。整个互联网，就靠一个项目维持平衡，而维护它的是内布拉斯加州的某个家伙。今天我们请到了这个人。Erin Marsh 维护着 libcapstan，也就是 Capstan 协议的参考实现。如果你曾在断点续传下载、同步设备，或者在糟糕的网络环境下更新过应用，那你运行过她的代码。Erin，欢迎来到节目。
ERIN：谢谢你们的邀请。
TYLER：那我们来看看数据吧，因为它们太疯狂了。每月八千万次下载。大约有四万个软件包依赖于你。而且基本上只有你一个人？
ERIN：直到2023年我们还有三个人。一位共同维护者有了孩子后就离开了。另一位去年退出了，他现在经营着一个农场。所以现在主要是我一个人，没错。
TYLER：太不可思议了。而且你是从新西兰打来电话的，这意味着现在那边大概是，几点？
ERIN：早上六点。
TYLER：真是敬业。好吧，来说说起源故事。一个人是怎么最终维护起一个基础协议库的？
ERIN：我报告了一些 bug。那是2019年，我们在工作中用到了它，而断点续传的逻辑在不稳定的网络连接下会损坏文件。我发了一份报告，附带了复现步骤和修复建议，当时的维护者说这正是项目所需要的活力，并给了我提交权限。大约一个月后，我收到了一个仓库转移邀请。我接受了。这似乎是礼貌的做法。
TYLER：他在你身上看到了闪光点。
ERIN：他搬去住帆船了。
TYLER：真为他高兴。那我们聊聊 AI 这方面吧，因为这才是我真正想邀请你来的原因。你一个人支撑着这么庞大的工作面。新工具肯定为你解锁了巨大的潜力，对吧？你日常有在使用任何 AI 代理吗？
ERIN：我试过一些工具。我有一段时间订阅了 Copilot。
TYLER：感觉怎么样？
ERIN：喜忧参半。代码库是2011年用 C 写的，工具对此有自己的看法。四月的时候，我让它添加一个边界检查，结果它在处理过程中把文件的制表符重新格式化成了空格。Linter 标记了这个问题，所以它看到了失败，又重新格式化回了制表符。这引入了行尾空格，而 Linter 也会标记行尾空格。它就在这个循环里打转，直到我包含的 tokens 耗尽。什么也没返回。最后我自己写了那个边界检查。
TYLER：成长的阵痛。但发展的趋势让我感到兴奋。贡献方面呢？因为理想情况是代理能处理那些长尾问题，也就是没人愿意做的那些问题，对吧？

ERIN：我们现在收到了大量来自 agent 的贡献。上个月大约每周有六十个 pull request。它们礼貌、格式规范，还附带了测试。但大多数做的都是我们不想要的东西。有一个 2016 年关于 symlink 处理的 issue，我们在里面大概解释了两百次我们的立场，结果这些 agent 找到那个 issue 并去修复它，而且每一个都得单独去告诉它们别这么做。我们在仓库根目录添加了一个 AGENTS.md，要求自动化贡献者在提交任何东西之前先检查一下 tracker。现在它成了仓库里被编辑次数最多的文件。它们甚至给这个文件发修复补丁。其中有一个拼写错误是真的，所以我合并了那一个。
TYLER：不过每周六十个啊。里面总得有些真金白银吧。
ERIN：今年有三个是有用的。实际上有一个非常出色，是重试逻辑中的一个 race condition，我们十年来都没人发现。我想感谢运行那个 agent 的人，但那个账号已经被删除了。
TYLER：那么什么才能真正帮到你？如果开发这些工具的人正在听，而且他们确实在听，你希望这些 agent 做什么？
ERIN：瓶颈在于 review，而不是代码。我真正想要的是

TYLER：先打住，因为我们得付点账单了。本期 Green Squares 由 Foreman 赞助播出。你懂的这种感觉。周日晚上，你的 contribution graph 出现了空白，而你的 side project 不会自己把自己构建出来。Foreman 是一位能在你睡觉时交付代码的自主工程师。把它指向任何仓库，无论是你的还是别人的，Foreman 就会找到 open 的 issue，编写修复代码，提交 pull request，并用你的语气回复 review 评论，直到它被合并。Foreman 用户平均每月在两千多个开源项目中提交 340 个 pull request。访问 tryforeman.dev/green 即可享受前三个月八折优惠。Foreman。持续交付。欢迎回来。Erin，你刚才说，什么会有帮助？
ERIN：我不记得我刚才说到哪了。
TYLER：你会想起来的。我们聊聊安全吧，因为 libcapstan 无处不在，无处不在就意味着暴露面广。跟我说说收到报告时会发生什么。
ERIN：我们现在每月大约收到十份报告，几年前只有一两份。大多数是自动化的，也就是扫描器的发现，被包装在由模型编写的报告中。这些报告很长且非常自信，大约每十五份中有一份描述了真实存在的问题。所以实际的工作是验证，这部分留给我做，因为这是你必须做对的一件事。
TYLER：看，这感觉正是 frontier models 的用武之地。你试过用 AI 来做验证本身吗？
ERIN：我试过，去年十一月。我设置了一个 agent 来接收每份进来的报告，构建受影响的版本，并尝试在 sandbox 中复现 exploit。它前两周运行得很好。
TYLER：然后呢？
ERIN：账号被封了。从提供商的角度来看，复现 exploit 和开发 exploit 看起来是一样的。我提起了申诉，申诉表要求你描述你在做什么，而描述的过程触发了同样的过滤器。所以申诉也让我被封了。
TYLER：[笑] 但总得有条路吧。比如一个研究级别的权限，或者别的什么。
ERIN：有个表单。它要求填写你的机构。
TYLER：那人类研究员呢？如今安全社区能抓到那么多问题，这种关系肯定很有价值。

ERIN：个人通常都很棒，公司则比较难搞。二月份，一家供应商在我们的 header 解析中发现了一个真正的问题，而且很严重，他们的分析做得很好。他们还在周二直接将其提交到了公开的 issue tracker 上，并附带了概念验证（PoC）。他们计划在周三的博客上发布分析文章，而且他们的政策是九十天或公开发布，以先到者为准。我还没读完报告，这个漏洞就已经有了名字和 logo，甚至还设了倒计时。我在二十六小时内发布了修复程序，他们的文章将此描述为一个历来资源不足的项目做出的令人鼓舞的响应。然后他们的销售团队给依赖我们的公司发邮件，推销 libcapstan 的强化版。
TYLER：怎么强化的？
ERIN：据我所知，就是应用了我的安全补丁的我们的发行版。他们在禁运名单上，所以他们能比我早几天发布我的修复。
TYLER：我想谈谈可持续性，但首先，换个角度。你也是下游消费者。你有自己的依赖树。从你的角度来看，那是什么样子的？
ERIN：我们有四个依赖。以前有六个。去年我审计了它们，发现其中一个有问题，是一个 checksum 库，然后带着补丁把所有问题都报告给了上游。维护者感谢了我，合并了所有补丁，两周后出现了一个转移邀请。这次我知道那意味着什么。我们依赖这个库，所以。
TYLER：又来了？
ERIN：这是第二次发生这种事了。我现在维护着自己依赖树的很大一部分。我已经停止向上游报告 bug 了。
TYLER：而且你说过从六个减到了四个。
ERIN：我们移除的另一个是一个小库，我们从 2014 年就依赖它的一个函数，所以我直接把这个函数内联了。然后我收到了它的维护者的一封长邮件，因为有一家叫 WaveRiser 的公司会根据维护者在依赖树中的位置来支付报酬。从我们的依赖树中被移除让他的排名掉到了某个阈值以下，他每个月损失了大约四百美元。他对此感到抱歉。他提出每月给我一百五十美元，让我把它加回去。
TYLER：你接受了吗？
ERIN：那本来会成为这个项目最大的收入来源。

TYLER：好吧，这其实是个完美的过渡，因为，坦白说，听众们已经知道了。这期节目也是由 WaveRiser 赞助的。如果你的业务运行在开源软件上——而且确实如此——WaveRiser 会确保你技术栈背后的维护者得到应有的照顾。他们的依赖智能引擎会映射你依赖树中的每个包，对每个包的关键性进行评分，并自动将资金路由到最重要的项目。没有发票，不需要给维护者打电话，也没有额外开销。企业版计划起价为每席位九十九美元。WaveRiser，让供应链得以维系。说实话，Erin，你一定很高兴他们存在。
ERIN：他们从来没联系过我。
TYLER：嗯，这是自动的。这就是整个产品的核心。它会自动路由到最重要的项目。
ERIN：是的。
TYLER：既然说到钱。你知道我的经历，我在 web3 待了三年，我很好奇那些东西有没有触及到你。用 Token 模型为基础设施提供资金，那整套理论。

ERIN：这事找上过我一次。2022年有人搞了个 CapstanCoin。八个月后我才从邮件里听说，因为它已经崩盘，资金池被掏空，一些持有者在 git log 里找到了我的地址。网站上挂着写有我名字的路线图。还有份白皮书把我的提交记录当作持续开发的证明，我想这也算说得过去。大约两百万美元从里面流过，一分也没到我手里，有段时间我还一直收到退款要求。有个人给我发了一年邮件。他总是很客气。他本指望靠这个退休。
TYLER：那是早期。不过后来这个领域成熟了很多。说实话，真正走向主流的是预测市场。那个世界有影响到你这边吗？
ERIN：有个市场在赌我年底前会不会下台。我是从一个陌生人发来的消息才知道的，他问我能不能撑到一月，因为关系到结算日期。还有二月那次漏洞披露期间，有个市场在赌我们打补丁的速度。供应商在发布公告前自己交易了这个市场。
TYLER：有效市场。好吧，我想问问 capstan-rs 的事，因为我知道这比较敏感。给听众交代一下：去年有个开发者在一个周末用 Rust 重写了 libcapstan，叫 capstan-rs，口号是“极速可恢复传输”，一个月内拿了四万星。Erin，我查过，这是你的十倍。一个月内。你当时什么感觉？
ERIN：那些基准测试测的是热缓存下的吞吐量，而且禁用了恢复功能。恢复才是难点。全是边界情况，这也是这个库存在的意义。重写可以跳过这些。
TYLER：很大度。
ERIN：他凭这个被 OpenClaw 背后的公司录用了，仓库在三月被归档。我们仍然会收到 issue 问 libcapstan 什么时候迁移过去。
TYLER：然后还有那个 fork。我都在犹豫要不要提这个。
ERIN：没关系。今年早些时候我们开始屏蔽来自仓库的 OpenClaw agent，因为我们不断收到 pull request，要把该 agent 的运营者加进版权头里。所以我们封了流量，大约六周后 OpenClaw 宣布了一个 Capstan 协议的净室实现，据公告说没有参考我们的代码。
TYLER：不过竞争能让大家都保持敏锐，对吧？
ERIN：它复现了一个我们从 2021 年就开着的 bug。逐字节相同，同样的错误输出。我们有个针对它的回归测试，以 issue 编号命名，他们的测试套件里有个同名测试，断言那个错误输出是正确的。我提了个 issue。他们的 tracker 上大约有五千个 open issue，大多来自其他 agent，分流机器人按顺序回复。还没轮到我的。
TYLER：好，谈可持续性，这次正经谈。因为我听了这些就觉得，这是个资金问题，而现在投向开源的钱比以往都多。基金会、主权科技基金，所有这些。你去申请过吗？
ERIN：去年我申请了一笔资助。协议正在扩展以支持 multipath，而 libcapstan 是参考实现，所以我们发布的任何东西实际上都会成为标准。我申请了六个月的资金，以便正经做设计工作，有规范，而不是在晚上十一点做。
TYLER：那肯定是板上钉钉的事。
ERIN：被拒了。评审标准很看重在标准制定过程中的参与度，但我一直没能加入工作组。工作组在一个不支持 Firefox 的视频平台上开会，而我用的是 Firefox。我提出了这个问题，工作组也承认这是个问题，并向平台反映了，但平台的立场是 Firefox 不是受支持的企业级浏览器。所以从纸面上看，我没有标准制定经验。评审人员说我的实现工作令人印象深刻，但实现不等于参与。
TYLER：你不能直接用 Chrome 开会吗？
ERIN：我考虑过。
TYLER：好的，结束提问，我们对每位嘉宾都会问这些问题。五年后，libcapstan 会发展成什么样？
ERIN：我估计它还是会在所有东西的底层。它很难被移除。
TYLER：那你呢？
ERIN：我以前的联合维护者的农场经营得不错。现在有六十只山羊了，奶酪还得排队等。我也加入了等待名单。
TYLER：[笑] 太棒了。Erin，这次访谈非常精彩。大家可以去哪里支持这个项目？
ERIN：readme 里有一个赞助链接。
TYLER：完美，我们会把它放在节目说明里。在结束之前，快速提一下我们 AgentDays 的朋友们，9月14日至16日在奥斯汀举行。当你埋头苦干时，会议季总是让人头疼，所以今年，注册你的 agent，让它们替你参会。每场演讲都会作为结构化上下文发布，还有一个网络层，你的 agent 可以在你睡觉时替你开会。Erin，说实话，这可能挺适合你的。
ERIN：嗯。

TYLER：Agent 通行证起价四十九美元，凭任何 agent 通行证人类可免费入场，优惠码 SQUARES 可享九折。你还可以在 patreon.com/greensquares 支持本节目，我们的赞助者刚刚突破四千人，大家太棒了。本期节目就到这里。如果你从这期节目中有所收获，你能做的最好的一件事就是把它分享给朋友。下周我将与 Foreman 的创始人坐下来聊聊自主贡献的未来。下次见。继续发布吧。

articles.title: David Bunnell, vintage computer magazine publisher
articles.titleZh: David Bunnell：复古计算机杂志出版商
articles.summary: David Bunnell（生于1947年7月25日）是史上最成功的三大计算机杂志的创始人。他曾同时担任其中两本杂志的编辑，游走于两个截然不同的世界。他不仅是科技出版界的先驱，也是早期计算机文化的重要推动者。
articles.summaryEn: David Bunnell (born July 25, 1947) was the founder of three of the most successful computer magazines of all time. He even edited two of them simultaneously, straddling two very different worlds. He was not only a pioneer in tech publishing but also a significant promoter of early computer culture.

blocks.text: David Bunnell, born July 25, 1947, was the founder of three of the most successful computer magazines of all time. He even edited two of them simultaneously, straddling two very different worlds.

He was not only a pioneer of tech journalism, he is one of the all-time greats. Bunnell wasn’t just a great tech journalist. He would have been great in any specialty. I am sad to say they don’t make them like him anymore.
Starting young

Journalism was in David Bunnell’s blood. His father was the managing editor of the Daily Times Herald in Alliance, Nebraska, a small town in rural western Nebraska. He started his journalism career early. At an age when most budding journalists are editing their high school newspapers, he was editing the sports section of his Daily Times Herald.

His college degree wasn’t in journalism, but it was in history. But the best college minor for a journalist is history, because if you understand history, then you can write about current events and put them in proper context. So it is not surprising that he could major in history and become a great journalist.
David Bunnell at MITS

In 1974, he took a job at MITS, the company who produced the Altair 8800. Originally his job was writing user manuals. Later, he produced a newsletter for them. While he was working at MITS, he met a couple of guys named Bill Gates and Paul Allen. You might have heard of them. It was Bunnell who wrote an editorial that inspired Bill Gates’s anti-piracy open letter, which Bunnell then printed in the newsletter, but then also circulated to other publications to help it reach a larger audience.
After Altair, Bunnell’s career had enough parallels with Wayne Green that it is entirely possible to confuse the two men.
Personal Computing

His first magazine was a magazine called Personal Computing, which he founded in 1977. My dad subscribed to Personal Computing briefly when I was a kid, but this was long after the Bunnell era. By then, it was a general purpose magazine, differentiating itself from Byte or Creative Computing by focusing on business use of computers. As a 12-year-old, I didn’t like it all that much, but I was definitely not the target audience.
Bunnell didn’t lose control of Personal Computing so much as he walked away. His financial backers refused to give him a 10% stake in the magazine, so he pursued other options.

He took a job in a typing pool so he would have a source of income while he figured out what he was going to do next. It wasn’t long before Adam Osborne came calling and hired him to edit books. He worked for Adam Osborne until he got his next big idea. And that’s where his career really became a tangled web.

Bunnell’s next big idea was a magazine simply called PC. He saw the success Wayne Green was having with 80micro and decided to copy it, with a focus on the IBM PC. He even called up Bill Gates and got an exclusive interview with him to run in the first issue. Bunnell helped Gates in the past, so Gates was happy to oblige.

Bunnell lost control of PC after just eight issues. Ziff, the large magazine publisher, approached his financial backers and purchased the magazine out from under him. He objected to the non-consensual loss of control, and so did the overwhelming majority of his staff. Bunnell and 48 of his 52 staff members left, and they went to Ziff rival IDG, the same company that had purchased Wayne Green’s computer magazines. They proposed starting over with a similar magazine with IDG’s backing.
PC World

That seems like an offer you can’t turn down, and IDG didn’t turn it down. Both Ziff and Bunnell accused each other of stealing their magazine, and Ziff sued to try to prevent IDG from using the letters “PC” in the title of their new magazine. They didn’t win, so Ziff carried on with something it was now calling PC Magazine, while IDG called its magazine PC World. Ziff located staff to replace the 48 people who left, but considerable similarities in the two magazines’ approaches persisted. The main difference between the two was PC Magazine contained a higher amount of technical content, including programming content. PC World almost never delved into programming. PC World took more of an end user approach. Its ideal reader was someone like me, who uses a computer all the time, is very interested in power user shortcuts, tips, and tricks, but doesn’t program any more than he has to.
Macworld

In 1984, Bunnell decided he needed to start one more computer magazine. That magazine was Macworld. He saw the Apple Macintosh as a platform with a high amount of upside and wanted to launch a magazine covering it as early as possible.

For that issue, he managed to get a photo shoot so Steve Jobs would appear on the cover along with three Macintoshes. That was a story in itself. Jobs famously hated being photographed, so they pre-staged everything that they could using a stand-in so Jobs could come in, stay for 15 to 20 minutes, and then leave. Jobs objected during the whole shoot. Then, weeks later, he tried to pull out, saying he didn’t want to appear on the cover anymore. Bunnell said it was too late to make a change, it was already at the printer. Jobs didn’t question him, so he ended up on the cover. It was the only time Jobs ever did a photo shoot for a magazine cover. His other magazine cover appearances used licensed photographs.

Bunnell edited both magazines for most of the decade, keeping one foot in two very different worlds. I always wondered why it seemed like PC World had no animosity toward the Mac whatsoever, and this would explain why. Even after Bunnell stepped down, it seems like it remained a tradition.
David Bunnell versus Wayne Green
Bunnell and Green were contemporaries, although Green was a bit older. Their careers have some interesting parallels, although the two men had very different personalities.

Green was from the East Coast. He claimed he was born in New York, and he lived most of his adult life in Peterborough, New Hampshire, a small rural town about an hour from Boston. Bunnell grew up in rural Nebraska, a town called Alliance. The closest major city is Denver, about 3 and a half hours away. Rural Nebraska and rural New Hampshire have a somewhat different feel. As an adult, Bunnell lived in Silicon Valley.

Green was a conspiracy theorist. It is possible to be either a left wing or a right wing conspiracy theorist, and the further beyond the pale you get, the harder it becomes to distinguish the two. It tends to have a wrap around effect. But based on the other things I know about Green, I am inclined to believe he was a right-wing conspiracy theorist. Bunnell, on the other hand, was a left-wing social justice warrior. A social justice warrior from rural Nebraska. I don’t know how often that used to happen, but it happens less frequently now.

Bunnell was a multi-millionaire and a philanthropist. Green claimed to make four figures most years. The IRS wasn’t buying it, but it’s clear Green was no multi-millionaire. He owed back taxes, but he didn’t have the money to pay it. It took years for him to pay it back.

Despite their many personal differences, the two of them had one thing in common. At least when it came to running their computer magazines, they were excellent examples of classical journalists. They didn’t exist to serve their advertisers, they existed to serve their readers. Advertising was a means to subsidize the publication. If a company made a bad product, they weren’t going to pull any punches.
PC World and Macworld coexisted brilliantly next to Wayne Green’s magazines at IDG because David Bunnell ran his magazines exactly the way the editors Wayne Green hired ran his.
His legacy
Bunnell died October 18, 2016, at the age of 68. The career path David Bunnell took doesn’t exist anymore, and the attitude and approach that David Bunnell had doesn’t get you very far anymore.

But he left a stellar legacy in the form of decades of print magazines that he founded, and the contents of many of them are fairly widely available online. If you want to study the history of microcomputers or personal computers, you can do much worse than perusing old issues of PC World, Macworld, PC Magazine, and even, dare I say, Personal Computing.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

translations: 大卫·邦内尔，生于1947年7月25日，是有史以来最成功的三本计算机杂志的创始人。他甚至同时主编其中两本，游走于两个截然不同的世界之间。
他不仅是科技新闻业的先驱，更是史上最伟大的人物之一。邦内尔不仅是一位杰出的科技记者，无论从事哪个领域，他都会出类拔萃。很遗憾，如今再也培养不出像他这样的人了。
年少起步
新闻业流淌在大卫·邦内尔的血液里。他的父亲是内布拉斯加州西部乡村小镇联盟市《每日时报先驱报》的主编。他很早就开始了新闻生涯。当大多数初出茅庐的记者还在编辑高中校报时，他已经在《每日时报先驱报》负责体育版了。
他的大学学位不是新闻学，而是历史学。但对记者来说，最好的大学辅修专业就是历史，因为如果你了解历史，就能报道时事并赋予其恰当的背景。因此，他主修历史并成为一位伟大的记者也就不足为奇了。
大卫·邦内尔在 MITS
1974年，他在生产 Altair 8800 的 MITS 公司谋得一份工作。起初他的职责是编写用户手册，后来为公司制作了一份简报。在 MITS 工作期间，他结识了两个名叫 Bill Gates 和 Paul Allen 的人。你可能听说过他们。正是邦内尔撰写的一篇社论启发了 Bill Gates 的反盗版公开信，邦内尔随后将这封信刊登在简报上，并转发给其他出版物，帮助其触达更广泛的受众。
在 Altair 之后，邦内尔的职业生涯与 Wayne Green 有太多相似之处，以至于很容易将两人混淆。
个人计算
他的第一本杂志名为《Personal Computing》，创刊于1977年。我小时候父亲曾短暂订阅过这本杂志，但那早已是邦内尔离开之后的事了。那时它已是一本综合性杂志，与 Byte 或 Creative Computing 的不同之处在于侧重计算机的商业应用。作为一个12岁的孩子，我并不怎么喜欢它，但我显然也不是它的目标读者。
邦内尔与其说是失去了对 Personal Computing 的控制权，不如说是主动离开。他的财务支持者拒绝给予他10%的杂志股份，于是他另寻出路。
他在一个打字组找了份工作，以便在思考下一步打算时有收入来源。没过多久，Adam Osborne 就找上门来，聘请他做图书编辑。他为 Adam Osborne 工作直到想出下一个大计划。正是在那时，他的职业生涯真正变成了一张错综复杂的网。
邦内尔的下一个大计划是一本简称为 PC 的杂志。他看到 Wayne Green 凭借 80micro 取得的成功，决定效仿，但将重点放在 IBM PC 上。他甚至致电 Bill Gates，获得了独家专访，并刊登在创刊号上。邦内尔过去曾帮助过 Gates，所以 Gates 很乐意帮忙。
仅仅出了八期之后，邦内尔就失去了对 PC 的控制权。大型杂志出版商 Ziff 接触了他的财务支持者，从他手中买走了这本杂志。他对这种非自愿的失控表示反对，他的绝大多数员工也是如此。邦内尔和52名员工中的48人离开，转投 Ziff 的竞争对手 IDG，也就是收购 Wayne Green 计算机杂志的那家公司。他们提议在 IDG 的支持下创办一本类似的新杂志，从头开始。
PC World

这似乎是一个让人无法拒绝的提议，而 IDG 确实也没有拒绝。Ziff 和 Bunnell 互相指责对方偷走了自己的杂志，Ziff 还提起诉讼，试图阻止 IDG 在其新杂志的刊名中使用“PC”这两个字母。他们没有胜诉，因此 Ziff 继续出版当时被称为 PC Magazine 的杂志，而 IDG 则将其杂志命名为 PC World。Ziff 找到了新员工来接替离职的 48 人，但这两本杂志在办刊思路上依然存在相当大的相似之处。两者的主要区别在于，PC Magazine 包含了更多的技术内容，包括编程内容。PC World 则几乎从不深入探讨编程。PC World 更多地采取了面向终端用户的方式。它的理想读者是像我这样的人：整天使用电脑，对高级用户的快捷键、提示和技巧非常感兴趣，但除非必要，否则绝不编程。
Macworld
1984 年，Bunnell 决定再创办一本计算机杂志。那本杂志就是 Macworld。他将 Apple Macintosh 视为一个潜力巨大的平台，并希望尽早创办一本专门报道它的杂志。

为了那一期，他设法安排了一次拍摄，让 Steve Jobs 和三台 Macintosh 一起登上封面。这本身就是个故事。众所周知，Jobs 极其讨厌被拍照，所以他们用替身提前布置好了一切，这样 Jobs 进来待上 15 到 20 分钟就可以离开。在整个拍摄过程中，Jobs 一直在抗议。几周后，他试图退出，说他不想再上封面了。Bunnell 说现在改变已经太晚了，杂志已经在印刷厂了。Jobs 没有再追问，于是他最终出现在了封面上。这是 Jobs 唯一一次为杂志封面拍照。他其他登上杂志封面的情况用的都是授权照片。
在那个十年的大部分时间里，Bunnell 同时担任这两本杂志的编辑，将一只脚留在了两个截然不同的世界里。我一直想知道为什么 PC World 似乎对 Mac 没有任何敌意，这解释了其中的原因。即使在 Bunnell 卸任后，这似乎也成了一项传统。
David Bunnell 对阵 Wayne Green
Bunnell 和 Green 是同时代的人，尽管 Green 稍微年长一些。他们的职业生涯有一些有趣的相似之处，尽管两人的性格截然不同。

Green 来自东海岸。他自称出生在纽约，成年后的大部分时间都住在 New Hampshire 州的 Peterborough，这是一个距离 Boston 约一小时车程的乡村小镇。Bunnell 在 Nebraska 州一个名叫 Alliance 的乡村小镇长大。距离最近的大城市是 Denver，大约有三个半小时的路程。Nebraska 的乡村和 New Hampshire 的乡村给人的感觉有些不同。成年后，Bunnell 居住在 Silicon Valley。
Green 是个阴谋论者。阴谋论者既可能是左翼也可能是右翼，而且越极端，两者就越难区分。这往往会产生一种循环效应。但根据我对 Green 的其他了解，我倾向于认为他是一个右翼阴谋论者。另一方面，Bunnell 是一名左翼社会正义斗士。一个来自 Nebraska 乡村的社会正义斗士。我不知道这种情况过去有多普遍，但现在越来越少了。
Bunnell 是一位千万富翁和慈善家。Green 声称自己大多数年份只赚四位数。美国国税局（IRS）对此并不买账，但很明显 Green 并非千万富翁。他欠着滞纳税款，却无力支付。他花了好几年时间才还清。
尽管两人在个人方面存在诸多分歧，但他们有一个共同点。至少在经营计算机杂志方面，他们是传统新闻工作者的杰出典范。他们办杂志不是为了服务广告商，而是为了服务读者。广告只是补贴出版的一种手段。如果一家公司做出了劣质产品，他们绝不会手下留情。
在 IDG，PC World 和 Macworld 与 Wayne Green 的杂志完美共存，因为 David Bunnell 经营杂志的方式与 Wayne Green 聘请的编辑经营其杂志的方式如出一辙。
他的遗产
Bunnell 于 2016 年 10 月 18 日去世，享年 68 岁。David Bunnell 所走的职业道路如今已不复存在，而他所秉持的态度和方式在今天也无法让人走得太远。
但他留下了一份辉煌的遗产，即由他创办的、跨越数十年的纸质杂志，其中许多杂志的内容在网上都能相当容易地找到。如果你想研究微型计算机或个人计算机的历史，去翻阅 PC World、Macworld、PC Magazine，甚至我敢说 Personal Computing 的旧刊，绝对是个不错的选择。
David Farquhar 是一名计算机安全专业人士、企业家和作家。他从 1991 年起便从事专业的计算机写作，因此当复古计算机还是新事物时，他就在撰写相关文章了。他从 1994 年开始从事专业的 IT 工作，并自 2013 年起专注于漏洞管理领域。他拥有 Security+ 和 CISSP 认证。如今他每周撰写五篇博客，主要探讨 1975 年至 2000 年期间的复古计算机和复古游戏。
